description: Atomic, provenance-tracked SEO and GEO knowledge for SEO Maker's AI grounding layer. Self-contained: items, controlled vocabularies, resolved policies and the source register are all in this file. Validate items against knowledge-item.schema.json.

usage.loadThis: The whole file. There is no companion CSV or JSONL.
usage.beforeAnswering: Filter items by checks/topic/applicability, drop status 'superseded' and 'needs_verification', then apply every policy in `policies` whose appliesToChecks or appliesToItems matches. A policy overrides an item's own phrasing.
usage.neverDo: Never emit a knowledgeType 'myth' item as a recommendation - it exists so the model contradicts the claim. Never phrase a recommendation more strongly than the item's evidenceStrength.

knowledgeType.authoritative: Official search-engine documentation, standards or specifications. Requires source.type official or standard.
knowledgeType.heuristic: Practitioner convention or reasonable best practice. Never present as an engine requirement.
knowledgeType.research: Peer-reviewed or preprint studies, experiments, benchmarks. Preserve method and population.
knowledgeType.myth: A claim the sources do not support. Exists so the model contradicts it. Never emit as a recommendation.

claimType.official_requirement: A standard or engine states a MUST.
claimType.documented_behavior: First-party description of how the system behaves.
claimType.specification_rule: Normative rule in a ratified standard.
claimType.evaluation_criterion: A rubric humans apply. NEVER describe as ranking-system behaviour.
claimType.experimental_result: Measured under a stated method. Never restate as causation.
claimType.correlation: Association only. Never restate as causation.

evidenceStrength.strong: First-party documentation or ratified standard, directly quoted.
evidenceStrength.moderate: Peer-reviewed research, or official documentation applied by inference.
evidenceStrength.weak: Single study, practitioner observation, or convention.

checks._note: CheckId values from packages/core/src/scoring/page-audit.ts, plus site-level audit surfaces.
checks.none: No deterministic check maps to this item; it is interpretation-only knowledge.

sourceSupport.derived: Follows from the source but is not stated in those words.
sourceSupport.insufficient: Do not rely on this item.

status.revised: Corrected in this pass; use freely. See provenance.migrationNote.
status.superseded: Replaced by supersededBy. EXCLUDE from retrieval.
status.needs_verification: Source not confirmed. EXCLUDE from retrieval and from user-facing output.

retrieval.routing: A deterministic finding maps to `checks` and `topic`. Filter by `applicability` for the feature in play, drop status 'superseded' and 'needs_verification', then order authoritative > research > heuristic. Route myth items to a contradiction slot, never a recommendation slot.
guardrails: Do not present a claimType 'evaluation_criterion' item as ranking-system behaviour.
Do not present 'experimental_result' or 'correlation' as causation.
Do not raise an item above its evidenceStrength when phrasing a recommendation.
Always carry `limitations` into any answer that uses the item.
Prefer provenance.verifiedAgainstLocalSource=true when two items cover the same ground.
Apply `governingPolicies` before emitting an item's recommendedAction.

policies.question: What does a page actually need to be eligible for Google's AI features?
policies.decision: Three conditions, all required: the page is indexed; it is eligible to be shown with a snippet; and the site is included in Search generative AI features in Search Console.
policies.rationale: Google's generative-AI guide (last updated 2026-07-10) is the most recently updated source and was read in full. It adds the Search Console condition that older guidance did not mention. The older position - that no special markup or AI-specific optimisation is needed - is not contradicted and is retained.
policies.directive: Verify indexability and snippet eligibility from the crawl. Then tell the user to confirm Search Console inclusion themselves, stating plainly that SEO Maker cannot check it. Never report a GEO readiness result as complete without naming that unchecked condition.
neverSay: There are no additional requirements beyond normal indexing.
Your site is eligible for AI Overviews. (SEO Maker cannot establish this.)
policies.losingClaim: No additional technical requirements exist beyond ordinary indexing and snippet eligibility.

policies.question: Which GEO content tactics should SEO Maker recommend?
policies.decision: Recommend verifiable substance - sources, quotations, data - and answer-first structure justified by reader benefit. Do not recommend rewriting content to sound more authoritative.
policies.rationale: The only controlled measurement of an authoritative-tone rewrite found no significant improvement. The same study found citations, quotations and statistics did help. Answer-first structure survives because Google independently endorses clear paragraphs, sections and headings for readers - but its supposed extraction mechanism is unconfirmed, so reader benefit is the only justification available.
policies.directive: Recommend adding sources, direct quotations and concrete data where claims are unsupported. Recommend stating the answer early and using clear headings, framed as helping readers. Decline tone-rewriting requests and explain that the measurement found no effect.
neverSay: Rewrite this in a more authoritative voice to improve AI visibility.
Answer-first structure makes your content easier for AI to extract. (No engine has confirmed this.)
policies.losingClaim: Writing in a more persuasive, authoritative style increases generative-engine visibility.

policies.question: May SEO Maker quote GEO effect sizes to users?
policies.decision: No. Describe direction, never a percentage.
policies.rationale: The widely quoted 40% comes from a pipeline the researchers built - top 5 Google results summarised by gpt-3.5-turbo - scored with metrics they defined themselves. On a real deployed engine the best result was 22%, and some methods reached only 9%. The effect also reversed by rank: low-ranked sources gained, the top-ranked source lost. A single number cannot honestly represent that.
policies.directive: Say that adding sources and data was measured to help content surface in generative engines, without attaching a figure. If a user cites a percentage, name the engine, the metric and the date it was measured on, and note that the benefit concentrated in lower-ranked pages.
neverSay: GEO tactics boost visibility by up to 40%.
This change will increase your AI visibility by X%.
policies.losingClaim: GEO methods reliably boost visibility by around 40% in generative engines.

policies.question: How should the h1 and h2 checks be reported?
policies.decision: As readability and accessibility observations. Never as a Google Search requirement or a ranking issue.
policies.rationale: Google states directly that heading order does not matter from a Google Search perspective and that there is no ideal number of headings. The single-H1 rule comes from accessibility practice, where semantic order genuinely matters, and was then misreported as a search requirement.
policies.directive: Keep running the h1 and h2 checks. Report a missing H1 as 'this page has no clear top-level heading for readers', and report heading structure as helping navigation and assistive technology. Lower the severity accordingly - this is not a ranking defect.
neverSay: Pages must have exactly one H1.
Skipped heading levels hurt your rankings.
Google requires a proper heading hierarchy.
policies.losingClaim: A page needs exactly one H1 and strictly ordered heading levels for Google.

policies.question: How should title and meta description length be reported?
policies.decision: As truncation risk only. Never as a pass/fail rule, and never as the lead finding.
policies.rationale: Google's title-link and snippet documentation specify no character limit. The stated title criteria are that it is unique to the page, clear, concise and accurately describes the content. Character ranges are display-truncation heuristics derived from SERP pixel budgets, which vary by device and character shape.
policies.directive: Lead with the documented criteria: is the title unique, clear, and accurate to what the page actually contains? Mention length only as 'this may be truncated in results', and advise putting the distinctive words first rather than hitting a count.
neverSay: Your title is too long. Keep it under 60 characters.
policies.losingClaim: Titles must be 50-60 characters and meta descriptions 120-160 characters.

policies.question: How should the word-count threshold be reported?
policies.decision: As an internal trigger only. Never surface the number or the threshold to the user.
policies.rationale: Three separate Google documents deny a preferred word count - 'No, we don't', 'no magical word count target', 'no ideal page length'. A threshold is still needed to make thinness computable, but it detects a candidate problem rather than defining a standard the page must meet.
policies.directive: When the threshold fires, read the page and report what is actually missing: an unanswered part of the topic, no first-hand detail, no supporting evidence. If the page is functional - a login, a converter, a category page - suppress the finding entirely, because page type does not determine quality.
policies.losingClaim: Pages need a minimum word count to perform in search.

policies.question: Should 410 be recommended over 404 to remove a page faster?
policies.decision: No. Recommend whichever status code is semantically correct, and make no speed claim.
policies.rationale: Google's documentation treats all 4xx codes except 429 identically for index removal. The belief that 410 is faster is long-standing practitioner convention, not current documentation.
policies.directive: Use 410 when the resource is permanently gone and 404 when it is simply not found. Do not attach a removal-speed expectation to either. For urgent removal, point the user at Search Console's removal tool instead.
neverSay: Return 410 instead of 404 to deindex this page faster.
policies.losingClaim: 410 Gone removes pages from the index faster than 404 Not Found.
policies.caveat: The supporting Google document is not archived in raw/ and was not re-read in this pass. The decision is safe either way, since it recommends semantic correctness rather than relying on the speed claim.

items.title: robots.txt controls crawling, and is defined by a formal standard
items.principle: The Robots Exclusion Protocol is a ratified IETF standard (RFC 9309) that defines how crawlers fetch and parse /robots.txt, including allow/disallow rule matching, the most-specific-rule precedence, a minimum parse size crawlers must honour, and caching behaviour.
items.explanation: Because the protocol is standardised, robots.txt syntax errors are objectively checkable rather than a matter of opinion. A deterministic check can compare a site's file against the standard's grammar and report concrete defects.
items.whyItMatters: Because the protocol is standardised, robots.txt syntax errors are objectively checkable rather than a matter of opinion. A deterministic check can compare a site's file against the standard's grammar and report concrete defects.

items.title: Unreachable robots.txt is handled differently from a missing one
items.principle: Under RFC 9309, a robots.txt that returns a client error (4xx) is treated as if no restrictions exist, while server errors or unreachable responses cause crawlers to assume crawling is disallowed for a period.
items.explanation: This makes a 5xx on robots.txt a more serious incident than a 404 on robots.txt. Persistent server errors on that one file can suppress crawling of an entire site.

items.title: robots.txt is defined by a ratified IETF standard, so syntax defects are objectively checkable
items.principle: The Robots Exclusion Protocol is an IETF Standards Track document (RFC 9309, September 2022) that specifies the robots.txt file's formal ABNF syntax, user-agent group matching, allow/disallow path matching, error handling, and caching behaviour.
items.explanation: Because the grammar and the matching algorithm are normative, a robots.txt finding can be reported as a standards violation with a citation rather than as a stylistic preference. SEO Maker's robots parser can compare a site's file against the specification and report concrete, defensible defects.
items.whyItMatters: It separates objective robots.txt defects (which the standard settles) from crawler-specific behaviour (which it does not), so recommendations do not overstate what is guaranteed.
appliesWhen: Auditing the syntax and structure of a site's /robots.txt
Explaining why a robots.txt construct is or is not valid
doesNotApplyWhen: Predicting whether a URL will be indexed - the standard governs crawling only
Reasoning about crawlers that do not implement RFC 9309, since compliance is voluntary
Reasoning about vendor extensions such as crawl-delay or wildcard behaviour beyond the specified set
items.recommendedAction: Report robots.txt defects against the RFC 9309 grammar and cite the relevant section, rather than describing them as best-practice deviations.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Abstract; Section 2 (Specification)
source.quote: This document specifies and extends the "Robots Exclusion Protocol" method originally defined by Martijn Koster in 1994 [...] Specifically, it adds definition language for the protocol, instructions for handling errors, and instructions for caching.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: The standard describes crawler behaviour only. It makes no claim about indexing, ranking, or how any individual search engine weights a disallowed URL, and compliance is voluntary for non-cooperative bots.

items.title: A 4xx on robots.txt means no restrictions apply
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.3.1.3 defines a robots.txt that returns an unavailable status (in HTTP, the 400-499 range) as "unavailable", and states that the crawler MAY then access any resources on the server.
items.explanation: A missing robots.txt is therefore a non-event for crawling: the site is fully crawlable by default. SEO Maker should not report a 404 on robots.txt as a crawl-blocking problem.
items.whyItMatters: It stops the tool raising a false alarm on the most common robots.txt state - absent - and keeps severity available for the 5xx case, which genuinely does suppress crawling.
appliesWhen: The crawl receives a 4xx response when fetching /robots.txt
Deciding the severity of a missing robots.txt finding
doesNotApplyWhen: The response is 429, which signals rate limiting rather than a permanently unavailable file
The response is 5xx or the host is unreachable - a different and stricter rule applies
items.recommendedAction: Treat a 4xx robots.txt as informational. Suggest publishing one only when the site actually needs crawl rules or wants to declare a sitemap, not as a defect to fix.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.3.1.3 ("Unavailable" Status), page 8
source.quote: If a server status code indicates that the robots.txt file is unavailable to the crawler, then the crawler MAY access any resources on the server.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: The standard permits full access but does not require it; a specific crawler may still apply its own conservative policy. It also says nothing about indexing consequences.

items.title: A 5xx or unreachable robots.txt means crawlers must assume complete disallow
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.3.1.4 states that if robots.txt is unreachable due to server or network errors (in HTTP, the 500-599 range), the file is undefined and the crawler MUST assume complete disallow. If it stays undefined for a reasonably long period - the standard gives 30 days as an example - crawlers MAY then treat it as unavailable or keep using a cached copy.
items.explanation: A server error on this single file can suppress crawling of an entire site, which makes it far more serious than a 404 on the same file. The 30-day allowance is a ceiling on the damage, not a reason to downgrade the finding.
items.whyItMatters: This is one of the few single-file failures that can take a whole site out of crawl. It deserves the highest technical severity SEO Maker can assign, and it is fully deterministic to detect.
appliesWhen: The crawl receives a 5xx response when fetching /robots.txt
The robots.txt host is unreachable due to DNS, TLS, or network failure
Site-wide crawl or indexing volume has dropped and robots.txt availability has not been ruled out
doesNotApplyWhen: The response is 4xx, which the standard treats as no restrictions
The error is transient and the file has since returned 200 - report it as history, not a live defect
items.recommendedAction: Escalate as a critical availability incident: make /robots.txt return 200 or 404, never 5xx. A static file or edge rule that cannot depend on the application backend is the usual fix.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.3.1.4 ("Unreachable" Status), page 8
source.quote: If the robots.txt file is unreachable due to server or network errors, this means the robots.txt file is undefined and the crawler MUST assume complete disallow.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: Exact retry windows, cache retention, and the point at which a crawler relaxes the assumption vary by implementation; the 30-day figure is an example in the standard, not a required threshold.

items.title: robots.txt is not access control, and listing a path exposes it
items.principle: RFC 9309 states that the rules are not a form of access authorization, and its Security Considerations section notes that listing paths in robots.txt exposes them publicly and thus makes them discoverable. Controlling access requires a real application-layer measure such as HTTP authentication.
items.explanation: Disallowing a path advertises that the path exists. When SEO Maker sees sensitive-looking paths in robots.txt - admin areas, staging hosts, internal exports - the correct advice is authentication or removal, never a tighter disallow rule.
items.whyItMatters: Recommending robots.txt as a way to hide content is actively harmful advice, and it is a common misconception among site owners.
appliesWhen: robots.txt contains paths that look private, administrative, or pre-production
A user asks how to keep a page out of search or away from the public
doesNotApplyWhen: The goal is genuinely crawl budget management on public URLs, where disallow is the right tool
relatedIssues: robots.txt used as a privacy control
items.recommendedAction: Where a disallowed path looks sensitive, recommend authentication or removal of the resource, and note that the robots.txt entry itself discloses the path.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 1 (Introduction) and Section 3 (Security Considerations), pages 3 and 9
source.quote: The Robots Exclusion Protocol is not a substitute for valid content security measures. Listing paths in the robots.txt file exposes them publicly and thus makes the paths discoverable.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: This is a statement about the protocol's guarantees, not a vulnerability assessment. SEO Maker cannot confirm from a crawl whether a disallowed path is actually sensitive or actually unprotected.

items.title: robots.txt must be at the top-level path, lowercase, UTF-8 and text/plain
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.3 requires the rules to be accessible in a file named "/robots.txt" (all lowercase) in the top-level path of the service, encoded as UTF-8 and served with the media type text/plain.
items.explanation: Each of these is a deterministic check with an unambiguous fix. A rules file at a subdirectory path, served as text/html, or in a non-UTF-8 encoding is not a valid robots.txt regardless of its contents.
items.whyItMatters: A robots.txt that is never read is indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so an otherwise correct rules file can be silently ineffective.
appliesWhen: Validating how a site serves its robots.txt
A site reports that its robots.txt rules are being ignored
doesNotApplyWhen: Evaluating the rules themselves rather than how the file is served
Per-protocol or per-host variants, where each scheme and authority has its own robots.txt
relatedIssues: robots.txt served with wrong content type
items.recommendedAction: Serve the file at the scheme-and-authority root as text/plain in UTF-8. Note that each host and scheme needs its own file.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.3 (Access Method), page 7
source.quote: The rules MUST be accessible in a file named "/robots.txt" (all lowercase) in the top-level path of the service. The file MUST be UTF-8 encoded [...] and Internet Media Type "text/plain".
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: Crawlers may be lenient in practice - some accept other content types - but leniency is not guaranteed by the standard and should not be relied on.

items.title: The most specific robots.txt rule wins, measured in octets, and allow breaks ties
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.2.2 requires that the most specific match be used, defines the most specific match as the one with the most octets, and states that where an allow rule and a disallow rule are equivalent the allow rule SHOULD be used. If no rule in the matching group matches, the URI is allowed, and /robots.txt itself is implicitly allowed.
items.explanation: Rule order in the file does not decide the outcome; rule length does. This is the single most misunderstood part of robots.txt, and it means a long Allow can legitimately override a short Disallow.
items.whyItMatters: Site owners frequently believe a later or earlier rule wins, and then either over-block or wrongly believe a path is blocked. Getting this right is what makes a blocked-URL explanation trustworthy.
appliesWhen: Explaining why a specific URL is or is not blocked by robots.txt
A site has overlapping Allow and Disallow rules for the same path prefix
doesNotApplyWhen: The user-agent group has not been resolved yet - group selection happens first
Reasoning about crawlers with non-standard matching behaviour
items.recommendedAction: When explaining a blocked URL, name the exact winning rule and its length rather than quoting the whole file. When a path must be opened, add an Allow rule longer than the competing Disallow.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.2.2 (The "Allow" and "Disallow" Lines), page 6; Section 5.2 (Longest Match), page 10
source.quote: The most specific match found MUST be used. The most specific match is the match that has the most octets. [...] If an "allow" rule and a "disallow" rule are equivalent, then the "allow" rule SHOULD be used.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: Path matching SHOULD be case sensitive and must start at the first octet, and percent-encoding is normalised before comparison - so naive string comparison can disagree with the specification.

items.title: Crawlers match one user-agent group, merging duplicates and falling back to the wildcard
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.2.1 requires case-insensitive matching of the product token; where several groups match the same token their rules MUST be combined into one group; if no group matches, the crawler MUST obey the group with the "*" user-agent if one is present; and if neither exists, no rules apply.
items.explanation: A crawler obeys exactly one effective group. Rules written for a different user agent never apply, which is why a site can have a large Disallow list and still be fully crawlable by a given bot.
items.whyItMatters: Reporting every Disallow line in a file as though it applied to Googlebot is a common and misleading tool behaviour. Group resolution has to happen before any blocking claim is made.
appliesWhen: A robots.txt contains multiple user-agent groups
Explaining which robots.txt rules actually govern a particular crawler
doesNotApplyWhen: Only one group exists and it is the wildcard group
Reasoning about crawlers that deliberately ignore robots.txt
relatedIssues: rules attributed to the wrong user agent
items.recommendedAction: Resolve the applicable group for the named crawler first, then report only that group's rules. State explicitly which user-agent group the finding applies to.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.2.1 (The User-Agent Line), pages 4-5
source.quote: If no matching group exists, crawlers MUST obey the group with a user-agent line with the "*" value, if present.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: The standard does not define behaviour for a crawler operating several product tokens, and search engines may run multiple distinct crawlers whose groups differ.

items.title: Crawlers must support #, $ and * in robots.txt rules
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.2.3 requires crawlers to support three special characters: "#" designating a line comment, "$" designating the end of the match pattern, and "*" designating zero or more instances of any character. To match these characters literally in a URI, crawlers SHOULD use percent-encoding.
items.explanation: Wildcard and end-anchor support is normative, not a Google extension, so patterns using them can be validated and explained with confidence. A rule intending to match a literal asterisk or dollar sign must percent-encode it.
items.whyItMatters: Wildcards are where robots.txt rules most often over-match and block more than intended, and SEO Maker can only explain that if it models the same semantics the standard defines.
appliesWhen: A robots.txt rule uses * or $
Explaining why a rule matched a broader set of URLs than the author expected
doesNotApplyWhen: Non-conforming crawlers that treat wildcards literally
Other robots.txt fields such as Sitemap, which are outside the allow/disallow grammar
items.recommendedAction: Expand wildcard rules against the crawled URL set and show which URLs a pattern actually matches, rather than reporting the pattern alone.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.2.3 (Special Characters), page 6
source.quote: Crawlers MUST support the following special characters: # [...] $ [...] *
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: The specification defines only these three characters. Any richer pattern syntax is a vendor extension with no standard guarantee.

items.title: robots.txt changes can take about a day to take effect
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.4 permits crawlers to cache robots.txt and states they SHOULD NOT use a cached version for more than 24 hours, unless the file is unreachable.
items.explanation: A robots.txt edit is not instant. When a site has just changed its rules, a crawl observing the old behaviour is expected rather than evidence of a defect.
items.whyItMatters: It sets the right expectation after a fix and prevents SEO Maker from reporting a stale-cache effect as an unresolved problem, or advising repeated re-crawls within the cache window.
appliesWhen: A site has recently edited robots.txt and is checking whether the change took effect
Explaining the expected delay after a robots.txt fix
doesNotApplyWhen: The file is unreachable, where crawlers may retain a cached copy for longer
Explaining delays in indexing, which are governed by different and much longer timescales
items.recommendedAction: After a robots.txt change, tell the user to allow roughly 24 hours before re-testing, and use standard HTTP cache-control headers if faster propagation matters.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.4 (Caching), page 9
source.quote: Crawlers SHOULD NOT use the cached version for more than 24 hours, unless the robots.txt file is unreachable.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: 24 hours is a SHOULD NOT ceiling, not a guarantee. Actual refresh intervals vary by crawler and by how often the host is crawled.

items.title: Crawlers must parse at least the first 500 kibibytes of robots.txt
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.5 states that crawlers SHOULD impose a parsing limit to protect their systems and that this limit MUST be at least 500 kibibytes.
items.explanation: Rules beyond roughly 500 KiB may never be read. A very large robots.txt is therefore a real risk to the rules at the bottom of the file, and file size is trivially measurable during a crawl.
items.whyItMatters: Large generated robots.txt files do occur on big ecommerce and faceted-navigation sites, and the resulting silent rule truncation is otherwise very hard to diagnose.
appliesWhen: The fetched robots.txt approaches or exceeds 500 KiB
A site's robots.txt is machine-generated from a large URL or parameter list
doesNotApplyWhen: Ordinary robots.txt files, which are far below the limit
items.recommendedAction: Flag a robots.txt approaching 500 KiB and recommend consolidating rules with wildcards so the important directives sit well inside the guaranteed parse window.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.5 (Limits), page 9
source.quote: Crawlers SHOULD impose a parsing limit to protect their systems [...] The parsing limit MUST be at least 500 kibibytes.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: 500 KiB is the minimum a crawler must honour, not a maximum it will read; a given crawler may parse more. The standard sets a floor, so the risk is a ceiling on guarantees, not a certainty of truncation.

items.title: robots.txt redirects are followed for at least five hops, then treated as unavailable
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.3.1.2 states that crawlers SHOULD follow at least five consecutive redirects, even across authorities; a robots.txt reached within five redirects MUST be fetched, parsed and applied in the context of the initial authority; beyond five, crawlers MAY assume the file is unavailable.
items.explanation: Redirecting robots.txt is permitted and the rules still bind to the original host. But a long redirect chain degrades to the unavailable case, which means no restrictions apply.
items.whyItMatters: Sites that centralise robots.txt behind redirects can silently lose their rules once the chain grows, and the failure mode - full crawlability - is the opposite of what the owner intended.
appliesWhen: The /robots.txt request is answered with one or more redirects
robots.txt is served from a different host than the site being audited
doesNotApplyWhen: robots.txt returns 200 directly
Reasoning about redirects on ordinary content URLs, which are governed by different guidance
items.recommendedAction: Record the full robots.txt redirect chain. Recommend serving the file directly at each host, and flag any chain approaching five hops.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.3.1.2 (Redirects), page 8
source.quote: The crawlers SHOULD follow at least five consecutive redirects, even across authorities [...] If there are more than five consecutive redirects, crawlers MAY assume that the robots.txt file is unavailable.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: Five is a SHOULD floor, so some crawlers follow more and some fewer. The rules apply in the context of the initial authority, which the standard states but individual implementations may handle differently.

items.title: Sitemap lines are outside the protocol and must not break user-agent groups
items.principle: RFC 9309 Section 2.2.4 states that crawlers MAY interpret records that are not part of the protocol, such as Sitemaps, and MAY be lenient about them - but parsing such records MUST NOT interfere with the defined records; specifically, a Sitemaps record MUST NOT terminate a group.
items.explanation: The Sitemap directive is a widely honoured convention, not part of the standardised rule grammar. Its placement inside a file does not reorganise the user-agent groups around it.
items.whyItMatters: Parsers that let a Sitemap line close a group produce wrong blocking answers, and a sitemap declaration is a useful discovery signal that should be read without being treated as a rule.
appliesWhen: Parsing a robots.txt that interleaves Sitemap lines with user-agent groups
Discovering sitemaps declared in robots.txt
doesNotApplyWhen: Judging whether the declared sitemap is valid or its URLs are indexable - that is separate analysis
relatedIssues: sitemap directive splitting a robots.txt group
items.recommendedAction: Read Sitemap directives for discovery but do not let them affect group parsing. Absence of a Sitemap line is a minor opportunity, not a rule violation.

source.name: RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol
source.location: Section 2.2.4 (Other Records), page 7
source.quote: Parsing of other records MUST NOT interfere with the parsing of explicitly defined records [...] For example, a "Sitemaps" record MUST NOT terminate a group.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Robots Exclusion Protocol.pdf

items.limitations: Because these records are outside the protocol, support and leniency vary by crawler, and the standard makes no promise that a declared sitemap will be fetched.

items.title: Google finds most pages by following links from pages it has already crawled
items.principle: Google states that it primarily finds pages through links from other pages it has already crawled, and that the vast majority of new pages it finds every day are discovered through links.
items.explanation: Internal linking is the primary discovery mechanism, not a secondary optimisation. A page with no inbound internal link depends entirely on weaker channels such as a sitemap.
items.whyItMatters: It gives orphan-page findings a first-party justification: the page is missing the main route by which Google discovers content.
appliesWhen: A crawled URL has zero internal inbound links
A URL appears in the sitemap or analytics but never as a crawl target
Explaining why new pages are slow to be discovered
doesNotApplyWhen: The page is deliberately excluded from indexing
Explaining why a discovered page was not indexed - discovery and indexing are different stages
items.recommendedAction: Link the page from related pages that are themselves crawled. Treat sitemap inclusion as a supplement to internal links, not a replacement.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Help Google find your content
source.quote: Google primarily finds pages through links from other pages it already crawled.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Discovery is not indexing: a well-linked page can still be excluded for quality, duplication or directive reasons. Google also discovers URLs through other channels it does not fully enumerate.

items.title: A sitemap is optional, and internal linking comes first
items.principle: Google describes submitting a sitemap as an optional technical step, notes that some CMSes generate one automatically, and says site owners should first focus on making sure people know about the site.
items.explanation: A missing sitemap is a low-priority opportunity, not a defect. Where a site has a discovery problem, internal linking is the higher-leverage fix.
items.whyItMatters: Tools routinely report a missing sitemap as a serious issue. Google's own framing puts it well below linking and promotion, which should shape how SEO Maker ranks the finding.
appliesWhen: A site has no XML sitemap
Prioritising discovery-related recommendations
doesNotApplyWhen: Large sites or sites with poorly linked sections, where sitemaps carry more weight
A sitemap exists but contradicts the site's indexing signals - that is a separate, real defect
items.recommendedAction: Report a missing sitemap as a low-severity opportunity. Recommend it confidently only for large sites, new sites, or sites with weakly linked sections.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Help Google find your content
source.quote: However this isn't required, and you should first focus on making sure people know about your site.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google's own sitemap documentation is more positive about sitemaps for large or poorly linked sites; this item is about baseline necessity, not about the value of a well-formed sitemap.

items.title: Blocking CSS or JavaScript can stop Google understanding a page
items.principle: Google states that when it crawls a page it should ideally see the page the same way an average user does, which requires access to the same resources as the user's browser. Hiding important components such as CSS and JavaScript may mean Google cannot understand the pages, so they might not show up in search results or rank well for the targeted terms.
items.explanation: A robots.txt rule that blocks an assets directory is not a harmless housekeeping choice - it can degrade how the page is understood. This is checkable by testing whether referenced CSS and JS URLs are disallowed.
items.whyItMatters: Blocked render resources are a common, invisible cause of poor indexing on JavaScript-heavy sites, and the fix is a one-line robots.txt change.
appliesWhen: robots.txt disallows paths containing the page's CSS or JavaScript resources
A JavaScript-rendered page indexes poorly or appears empty in rendering tests
doesNotApplyWhen: Blocked resources that do not affect layout or main content, such as analytics beacons
Third-party resources the site does not control
items.recommendedAction: Cross-check referenced CSS and JS URLs against robots.txt rules and recommend unblocking any resource needed to render main content. Verify with Search Console's URL Inspection tool.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Check if Google can see your page the same way a user does
source.quote: If your site is hiding important components that make up your website (like CSS and JavaScript), Google might not be able to understand your pages, which means they might not show up in search results or rank well for the terms you're targeting.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google says it might not understand the page, not that it definitely will not. The impact depends on how much of the main content depends on the blocked resource.

items.title: Google's crawler generally requests from a US location
items.principle: Google states that if pages show different information depending on the user's physical location, site owners should be satisfied with what Google sees from its crawler's location, which is generally the US.
items.explanation: Geo-redirects and location-gated content can hide the real page from the crawler. A site that redirects non-local visitors, or serves a country picker instead of content, may be indexed on the wrong version.
items.whyItMatters: It explains a whole class of otherwise baffling indexing problems on international and localised sites, and it is directly testable by comparing crawled content against what a local user sees.
appliesWhen: A site geo-redirects or varies content by visitor location
A non-US site reports that the wrong locale version is indexed
Auditing an international or multi-region site
doesNotApplyWhen: Sites that serve identical content regardless of location
Reasoning about which locale version ranks for a given user, which hreflang governs
items.recommendedAction: Avoid automatic geo-redirects for crawlers. Serve each locale on its own crawlable URL and connect them with hreflang rather than redirecting by IP.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Check if Google can see your page the same way a user does
source.quote: If your pages have different information depending on the user's physical location, make sure you're satisfied with the information that Google sees from its crawler's location, which is generally the US.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google says the crawl location is generally the US, not always; it does crawl from other locations in some circumstances. SEO Maker's own crawler location may differ from Google's, so findings are indicative.

items.title: Words in a URL help users, mainly through breadcrumbs
items.principle: Google states that parts of the URL can be displayed in search results as breadcrumbs, so users can use URLs to judge whether a result will be useful, and recommends including words in the URL that may be useful for users. A URL containing only random identifiers is described as less helpful.
items.explanation: The benefit Google names is user comprehension and breadcrumb display, not ranking. SEO Maker should frame URL recommendations that way and avoid implying that keywords in URLs carry ranking weight.
items.whyItMatters: It lets the tool recommend readable URLs honestly, while staying consistent with Google's separate statement that keywords in the URL path have hardly any ranking effect.
appliesWhen: URLs consist of opaque IDs, hashes, or session parameters
Advising on URL structure for new sections of a site
doesNotApplyWhen: Existing indexed URLs where changing the URL would require redirects and risk disruption for a cosmetic gain
Any claim that adding keywords to a URL will improve ranking
items.recommendedAction: Recommend descriptive URLs for new URLs, and explicitly note that rewriting established URLs is rarely worth the redirect risk.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Use descriptive URLs
source.quote: Parts of the URL can be displayed in search results as breadcrumbs, so users can also use the URLs to understand whether a result will be useful for them.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google states separately that keywords in the domain name or URL path alone have hardly any ranking effect beyond appearing in breadcrumbs. The benefit is user-facing.

items.title: Directory grouping helps Google learn how often sections change
items.principle: Google states that if a site has more than a few thousand URLs, how content is organised may affect crawling and indexing: using directories to group similar topics helps Google learn how often the URLs in individual directories change, and it can then crawl different directories at different frequencies.
items.explanation: This is a crawl-efficiency mechanism with an explicit size condition. Below roughly a few thousand URLs Google presents it as unimportant, so the recommendation should be gated on site size.
items.whyItMatters: It gives SEO Maker a principled, source-backed threshold for when site-structure advice is worth raising at all, instead of recommending reorganisation to every site.
appliesWhen: The site has more than a few thousand URLs
Sections of the site change at very different rates, such as policies versus promotions
Auditing a large ecommerce or publisher site
doesNotApplyWhen: Small sites, where Google explicitly says search engines will likely understand the pages as they are
Recommending a wholesale restructure of an existing site, which Google advises against doing reactively
relatedIssues: flat URL structure on a large site
items.recommendedAction: For large sites only, recommend grouping topically similar pages into directories whose change frequency is consistent. Say plainly that small sites do not need this.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Group topically similar pages in directories
source.quote: If you have more than a few thousand URLs on your site, how you organize your content may have effects on how Google crawls and indexes your site.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google gives no precise URL count and describes the effect on crawl scheduling, not on ranking. It also warns against dropping everything to reorganise an existing site.

items.title: Duplicate content is inefficient, not a penalty
items.principle: Google states that having duplicate content on a site is not a violation of its spam policies and will not cause a manual action, but that it can be a bad user experience and search engines might waste crawling resources on URLs the owner does not care about. Copying other people's content is treated differently.
items.explanation: Duplicate content findings should be framed as crawl waste and user confusion. The word penalty should not appear, because Google explicitly rules it out for a site's own duplicates.
items.whyItMatters: The duplicate content penalty is one of the most persistent myths in SEO, and tools reinforce it. Correct framing changes both the severity and the recommended fix.
appliesWhen: The same content is reachable at multiple URLs on the same site
A user asks whether duplicate content will hurt their rankings
doesNotApplyWhen: Content scraped or copied from other sites, which Google's scraped-content spam policy does cover
Large-scale duplication produced to manipulate rankings, which falls under scaled content abuse
items.recommendedAction: Report duplication as wasted crawl and a confusing experience. Recommend a redirect where possible and rel=canonical where it is not, and state that no penalty is involved.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Reduce duplicate content
source.quote: Having duplicate content on your site is not a violation of our spam policies, but it can be a bad user experience and search engines might waste crawling resources on URLs that you don't even care about.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: This covers a site's own duplicate URLs. It does not license republishing other sites' content, and it does not mean duplication has no cost.

items.title: Prefer a redirect over rel=canonical when consolidating duplicates
items.principle: Google's starter guide advises that where multiple pages hold the same information, site owners should try setting up a redirect from the non-preferred URLs to the URL that best represents the information, and use the rel=canonical link element only if they cannot redirect.
items.explanation: This gives an explicit ordering for a very common recommendation. Where a duplicate URL serves no independent purpose, redirecting is the stronger and preferred remedy.
items.whyItMatters: SEO Maker often detects duplicates without a canonical. Knowing Google's preferred order means the recommendation can be specific rather than offering two equivalent options.
appliesWhen: Several URLs serve the same content and only one needs to exist
A duplicate cluster has no canonical annotation
doesNotApplyWhen: The duplicate URL must stay reachable, for example a print view, a tracked campaign URL, or a variant users navigate to directly
Cross-domain duplication where redirecting would remove a page the other party needs
items.recommendedAction: Recommend a redirect to the preferred URL first; recommend rel=canonical as the fallback when the duplicate must remain reachable.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Reduce duplicate content
source.quote: If you have multiple pages that have the same information, try setting up a redirect from non-preferred URLs to a URL that best represents that information. If you can't redirect, use the rel="canonical" link element instead.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google also notes that if the owner does not canonicalise, it will try to do so automatically, and advises not to worry too much about this. The advice is about which tool is stronger, not about urgency.

items.title: A good title is unique to the page, clear, concise and accurate
items.principle: Google states that site owners influence title links by writing good titles, and defines a good title as one that is unique to the page, clear and concise, and accurately describes the contents of the page. It suggests a title may include the site or business name, the business location, and what the page offers.
items.explanation: These four properties - unique, clear, concise, accurate - are the criteria SEO Maker should evaluate and generate titles against. None of them is a character count.
items.whyItMatters: It gives title analysis a first-party rubric, replacing the character-count heuristic that dominates SEO tooling and that Google's own documentation does not support.
appliesWhen: Evaluating an existing title element
Generating a replacement title for a page
A title is duplicated across several pages
doesNotApplyWhen: Predicting whether Google will rewrite the title, which Google does not publish rules for
Treating any specific length as a pass or fail condition
items.recommendedAction: Score titles on uniqueness, clarity, concision and accuracy against the page's actual content. Report length only as truncation risk, never as a rule violation.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Influence your title links
source.quote: a good title is unique to the page, clear and concise, and accurately describes the contents of the page
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google's title-link documentation states no character limit, and Google may rewrite the title link regardless of how well the title element is written.

items.title: A good meta description is short, unique to one page, and carries the page's key points
items.principle: Google states that the snippet is sourced from the actual content of the page, that occasionally it may come from the meta description tag, and that a good meta description is short, unique to one particular page, and includes the most relevant points of the page.
items.explanation: Uniqueness and relevance are the criteria. Because the snippet usually comes from page content, a missing meta description is a missed opportunity rather than a broken page.
items.whyItMatters: It lets SEO Maker generate and evaluate descriptions against stated criteria, and calibrate the severity of a missing description correctly.
appliesWhen: A page has no meta description or shares one with other pages
Generating a meta description for a page
doesNotApplyWhen: Claiming the meta description influences ranking
Enforcing a specific character count as a rule
items.recommendedAction: Write a unique description per page covering its most relevant points. Report length only as truncation risk.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Control your snippets
source.quote: A good meta description is short, unique to one particular page, and includes the most relevant points of the page.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Because snippets are generated per query and mostly from page content, a written description may be ignored for most queries. Google publishes no length limit.

items.title: Text near an image helps Google understand what the image means on the page
items.principle: Google recommends using images that are sharp and clear and placing them near text that is relevant to the image, stating that the text near images can help Google better understand what the image is about and what it means in context to the page.
items.explanation: Image understanding is not carried by the alt attribute alone. Placement relative to related text is a separate, stated factor, which matters for pages that group all images away from the prose.
items.whyItMatters: It extends image recommendations beyond alt text, and gives a reason to flag galleries and carousels that separate images from their explanatory content.
appliesWhen: A page has images placed away from the text that explains them
Auditing image usage on content or product pages
doesNotApplyWhen: Purely decorative images, which should carry an empty alt attribute and need no surrounding context
Pages where image discovery is irrelevant to the site's goals
items.recommendedAction: Recommend placing each meaningful image next to the text that describes it, in addition to writing descriptive alt text.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Add high-quality images near relevant text
source.quote: The text that's near images can help Google better understand what the image is about and what it means in context to your page.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google describes this as helping it understand the image; it does not quantify the effect or promise image-search visibility.

items.title: Alt text explains the relationship between the image and the page's content
items.principle: Google describes alt text as a short but descriptive piece of text that explains the relationship between the image and the content, and states that it helps search engines understand what the image is about and the context of how it relates to the page.
items.explanation: The test for good alt text is relational: does it explain what this image is doing on this page. That is a content judgement, so it belongs to the AI layer rather than the presence-or-absence check.
items.whyItMatters: It lets SEO Maker move past counting missing alt attributes and assess whether the alt text present is actually useful.
appliesWhen: Images have alt attributes whose usefulness needs judging
Generating alt text suggestions for meaningful images
doesNotApplyWhen: Decorative images, which take an empty alt attribute
Deciding alt text from the filename alone, without the page context
items.recommendedAction: Judge alt text on whether it describes the image's role in this page's content, and rewrite it descriptively rather than inserting target keywords.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Add descriptive alt text to the image
source.quote: Alt text is a short, but descriptive piece of text that explains the relationship between the image and your content.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Correct alt text depends on the image's role on the page, which an automated check cannot fully determine. Accessibility, not search, is the primary reason the attribute exists.

items.title: Qualify links you do not vouch for, and automate that for user-generated content
items.principle: Google advises that when linking to pages outside your control you should trust the resource, and that if you cannot trust it but still want to link, you should add a nofollow or similar annotation to avoid search engines associating your site with it. For user-generated content such as forum posts or comments, Google says every user-posted link should have such an annotation added automatically by the CMS.
items.explanation: This is a site-configuration recommendation with a concrete trigger: any surface that accepts user-submitted links. Google explicitly ties it to avoiding negative ranking consequences.
items.whyItMatters: Sites with open comments or forums accumulate untrusted outbound links silently, and the fix is a template or CMS setting rather than manual clean-up.
appliesWhen: The site accepts user-generated content containing links
A page links out to sites the owner does not control or vouch for
doesNotApplyWhen: Editorial outbound links to trusted sources, which Google encourages as corroboration
Internal links within the same site
items.recommendedAction: Where the site accepts user-submitted links, recommend automatic nofollow or ugc annotation in the CMS. For editorial outbound links, recommend annotation only where the destination is not vouched for.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Link when you need to
source.quote: If you're accepting user-generated content on your site, such as forum posts or comments, make sure every link that's posted by users has a nofollow or similar annotation automatically added by your CMS.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google frames this as avoiding association and potential negative consequences; it does not quantify the risk. Annotating trusted editorial links is unnecessary.

items.title: Google names four attributes of compelling and useful content
items.principle: Google states that creating compelling and useful content will likely influence a site's presence in search results more than any other suggestion in its starter guide, and lists four shared attributes: the text is easy to read and well organised; the content is unique; the content is up to date; and the content is helpful, reliable and people-first.
items.explanation: These four attributes are a compact, first-party content rubric, and Google ranks content above every technical suggestion in the same guide. That ordering should inform how SEO Maker prioritises findings.
items.whyItMatters: It grounds content recommendations in official documentation and supports putting content problems above minor technical ones when both appear in the same audit.
appliesWhen: Assessing whether a page's content is adequate for its purpose
Ordering a mixed list of content and technical recommendations
doesNotApplyWhen: Treating these attributes as measurable scores - they are qualitative
Pages whose purpose is transactional or functional rather than informational
items.recommendedAction: Assess content against readability and organisation, uniqueness, currency, and helpfulness, and present content findings above minor technical ones.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Make your site interesting and useful
source.quote: Creating content that people find compelling and useful will likely influence your website's presence in search results more than any of the other suggestions in this guide.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Qualitative attributes with no published measurement. Google says some suggestions may not apply to a given business.

items.title: Different audiences use different words, but Google does not need every variant
items.principle: Google advises anticipating that users with different topic familiarity search differently - its example is charcuterie versus cheese board - while also stating that site owners should not worry about anticipating every variation, because Google's language matching systems can understand how a page relates to many queries even when the exact terms are absent.
items.explanation: Both halves matter. Vocabulary awareness is useful when it reflects real audience differences; producing variants to cover phrasings is explicitly unnecessary.
items.whyItMatters: It separates legitimate audience-vocabulary advice from keyword-variant page generation, which Google treats elsewhere as scaled content abuse.
appliesWhen: A page's terminology may not match how its audience actually searches
A user asks whether to create pages for query variations
doesNotApplyWhen: Recommending near-duplicate pages per keyword variant
Any keyword-density or exact-match reasoning
items.recommendedAction: Suggest natural vocabulary that matches the audience, and state explicitly that separate pages for query variants are not needed and may be treated as scaled content abuse.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Expect your readers' search terms
source.quote: Google's language matching systems are sophisticated and can understand how your page relates to many queries, even if you don't explicitly use the exact terms in them.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google gives no guidance on how far its language matching extends, so this cannot be used to argue that wording never matters.

items.title: SEO changes take hours to months to show up, and not all changes show up at all
items.principle: Google states that every change takes some time to be reflected, that some changes might take effect in a few hours while others could take several months, that site owners should generally wait a few weeks before assessing whether work had beneficial effects, and that not all changes will produce a noticeable impact in search results.
items.explanation: This is the expectation-setting SEO Maker should attach to any recommendation it makes, and the reason it should not promise outcomes or timelines.
items.whyItMatters: Users interpret an unchanged metric a week after a fix as failure. A first-party statement about latency prevents both premature conclusions and overpromising in the tool's own language.
appliesWhen: Reporting what a user should expect after applying a recommendation
A user asks how long a fix will take to work
Comparing crawls taken a short time apart
doesNotApplyWhen: Technical states that are immediately verifiable, such as whether a status code or tag changed
items.recommendedAction: Attach an explicit latency caveat to recommendations, and avoid presenting any expected ranking or traffic outcome or date.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: How long until I see impact in search results?
source.quote: Some changes might take effect in a few hours, others could take several months. In general, you likely want to wait a few weeks to assess whether your work had beneficial effects in Google Search results.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google gives ranges rather than commitments and does not say which change types are fast or slow.

items.title: Myth: the meta keywords tag affects Google rankings
items.principle: Claim: populating the keywords meta tag helps a page rank. Reality: Google states plainly that Google Search does not use the keywords meta tag, and lists it among the things site owners should not focus on.
items.explanation: If SEO Maker detects a meta keywords tag, it should be reported as inert - neither a defect nor an optimisation. Never recommend adding or populating one.
items.whyItMatters: Legacy CMS templates still emit this tag and legacy audit tools still flag it as missing, which wastes user effort on a tag with no effect.
appliesWhen: A page contains a keywords meta tag
A user asks whether to fill in meta keywords
doesNotApplyWhen: Other search engines or internal site-search systems that may use the tag
items.recommendedAction: State that Google Search does not use this tag. Do not recommend adding, removing or populating it for Google's sake.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on
source.quote: Google Search doesn't use the keywords meta tag.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: The statement is about Google Search. Some other systems may read the tag, and leaving it in place is harmless.

items.title: Myth: keywords in the domain name or URL path improve rankings
items.principle: Claim: putting target keywords in the domain or URL path improves ranking. Reality: Google states that from a ranking perspective the keywords in the domain name or URL path alone have hardly any effect beyond appearing in breadcrumbs, and recommends choosing a site name by general marketing best practices.
items.explanation: URL readability should be recommended for user comprehension and breadcrumb display only. Exact-match domains and keyword-stuffed slugs are not ranking improvements.
items.whyItMatters: URL rewrites are expensive and risky. Recommending them for a ranking benefit Google says is negligible trades real redirect risk for nothing.
appliesWhen: A user asks about exact-match domains or keyword-rich slugs
Considering whether to rewrite existing URLs
doesNotApplyWhen: Recommending readable URLs for new pages, where the user-facing benefit still stands
items.recommendedAction: Recommend descriptive URLs for user clarity, and say explicitly that keyword placement in the URL is not a meaningful ranking lever.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on - Keywords in the domain name or URL path
source.quote: From a ranking perspective, the keywords in the name of the domain (or URL path) alone have hardly any effect beyond appearing in breadcrumbs.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google says hardly any effect rather than none, and URL words do appear in breadcrumbs, which has a genuine user-facing value.

items.title: Myth: the TLD affects how Google ranks a site
items.principle: Claim: some top-level domains rank better than others. Reality: Google states the TLD only matters if you are targeting a specific country's users, and even then it is usually a low impact signal; otherwise Google Search does not care which TLD is used.
items.explanation: Domain extension is a business and country-targeting decision. SEO Maker should not raise a site's TLD as a ranking concern.
items.whyItMatters: Domain migrations are among the riskiest changes a site can make, and TLD-based ranking claims are a common reason they get proposed.
appliesWhen: A user asks whether to move to a different TLD for SEO reasons
Auditing a site on a newer or less common TLD
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuine single-country targeting, where a country-code TLD does carry a documented, low-impact signal
items.recommendedAction: Do not recommend a TLD change for ranking. Discuss country-code TLDs only in an explicit country-targeting context, and note the impact is low.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on - Keywords in the domain name or URL path
source.quote: the TLD (the domain name ending like ".com" or ".guru") only matters if you're targeting a specific country's users, and even then it's usually a low impact signal.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Country-code TLDs do carry a geotargeting signal that Google describes as usually low impact, so the answer is not a flat no in an international context.

items.title: Myth: Google requires one H1 and a strict heading order
items.principle: Claim: a page must have exactly one H1 and headings must descend without skipping levels for Google. Reality: Google states that having headings in semantic order is fantastic for screen readers, but from a Google Search perspective it does not matter if they are used out of order, and that there is no magical, ideal amount of headings a page should have - though if you think it is too much, it probably is.
items.explanation: Heading findings should be framed as accessibility and reader clarity, which is where Google locates the benefit, not as a Google Search requirement. A missing or duplicated H1 is not a ranking defect.
items.whyItMatters: The single-H1 rule is one of the most widely enforced fictions in SEO tooling, and SEO Maker's own deterministic layer includes an h1 check whose wording the AI layer must not escalate into a Google rule.
appliesWhen: A page has zero, multiple, or out-of-order headings
Reporting the result of an h1 or h2 check
A user asks how many H1s a page should have
doesNotApplyWhen: Accessibility reviews, where semantic heading order genuinely matters for assistive technology
Pages where headings are so sparse that readers cannot navigate the content, which is a real usability problem
items.recommendedAction: Report heading structure as a readability and accessibility matter. Do not describe a missing or duplicated H1 as a Google Search requirement or a ranking problem.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on - Number and order of headings
source.quote: Having your headings in semantic order is fantastic for screen readers, but from Google Search perspective, it doesn't matter if you're using them out of order. [...] There's also no magical, ideal amount of headings a given page should have.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google's statement concerns order and count. Headings still matter for users and assistive technology, and Google separately recommends headings that give clear structure to content.

items.title: Myth: E-E-A-T is a ranking factor
items.principle: Claim: E-E-A-T is a ranking factor that can be measured and optimised. Reality: Google's starter guide lists "Thinking E-E-A-T is a ranking factor" under things not to focus on and answers "No, it's not"; the helpful-content guidance states that while E-E-A-T itself is not a specific ranking factor, Google uses a mix of factors that can identify content with good E-E-A-T.
items.explanation: E-E-A-T is a vocabulary for discussing credibility, not a score. SEO Maker may use it to explain a content-credibility recommendation but must never present it as a measurable factor or report an E-E-A-T score.
items.whyItMatters: Selling an E-E-A-T score is a common tooling overreach. Two separate Google documents contradict it directly, which makes this one of the safest corrections the AI layer can make.
appliesWhen: A user asks how to improve or measure their E-E-A-T
Explaining content credibility recommendations
A third-party report has assigned the site an E-E-A-T score
doesNotApplyWhen: Discussing the concrete practices E-E-A-T describes - authorship, sourcing, first-hand experience - which Google does encourage
items.recommendedAction: Use E-E-A-T as explanatory vocabulary only. Recommend the underlying practices, and state that Google says E-E-A-T is not itself a ranking factor.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on - Thinking E-E-A-T is a ranking factor
source.quote: Thinking E-E-A-T is a ranking factor. No, it's not.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google does say it uses a mix of factors that identify content with good E-E-A-T, and gives such content more weight on YMYL topics - so the underlying concepts are not irrelevant.

items.title: Myth: duplicate content triggers a penalty
items.principle: Claim: duplicate content on a site causes a ranking penalty. Reality: Google states that content accessible under multiple URLs is fine, that it is inefficient but not something that will cause a manual action, and that copying other people's content is a different matter.
items.explanation: Report duplication in terms of crawl waste and user confusion. The correct fix is consolidation, and the correct urgency is low unless the duplication is large enough to affect crawl coverage.
items.whyItMatters: Overstated duplicate-content warnings push users into unnecessary and sometimes damaging canonical or redirect changes.
appliesWhen: The same content is reachable at several URLs on one site
A user asks whether duplicate content will get them penalised
doesNotApplyWhen: Content copied from other sites, which Google's scraped-content policy does address
Mass-generated near-duplicate pages, which fall under scaled content abuse
items.recommendedAction: Say plainly that there is no duplicate content penalty for a site's own duplicates, then recommend consolidation for crawl efficiency and clarity.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on - Duplicate content "penalty"
source.quote: If you have some content that's accessible under multiple URLs, it's fine; don't fret about it. It's inefficient, but it's not something that will cause a manual action.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Inefficiency is real: duplication wastes crawl resources and can leave the wrong URL indexed. Copied third-party content is a separate and genuine risk.

items.title: Myth: subdirectories beat subdomains for SEO
items.principle: Claim: content must live in subdirectories rather than subdomains to perform in search. Reality: Google says to do whatever makes sense for your business - it may be easier to manage a site segmented by subdirectories, and other times it may make sense to partition topics into subdomains.
items.explanation: This is an operational choice, not an SEO rule. A subdomain migration proposed purely for ranking has no first-party support and carries real migration risk.
items.whyItMatters: Subdomain-to-subdirectory migrations are expensive, disruptive, and frequently recommended on the strength of this myth alone.
appliesWhen: A site uses subdomains for blog, docs, shop or similar sections
A user asks whether to migrate a subdomain into a subdirectory
doesNotApplyWhen: Cases with a concrete operational reason to consolidate, such as shared templates or analytics
items.recommendedAction: Present the choice as operational. Do not recommend a migration on ranking grounds, and note that each subdomain needs its own robots.txt and sitemap handling.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on - Subdomains versus subdirectories
source.quote: From a business point of view, do whatever makes sense for your business.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Subdomains do have practical consequences for robots.txt scope, sitemap organisation and analytics, which are legitimate reasons to prefer one arrangement.

items.title: Myth: links and PageRank are what Google ranking comes down to
items.principle: Claim: rankings are essentially a function of links. Reality: Google states that while PageRank uses links and is one of its fundamental algorithms, there is much more to Google Search than just links, and that it has many ranking signals of which PageRank is just one.
items.explanation: Link-centric explanations should not be offered as the default reason a page underperforms, especially when SEO Maker has direct evidence of content, intent or technical problems.
items.whyItMatters: Link-only diagnoses send users toward link acquisition when the observable problem is usually something the tool can actually see and fix.
appliesWhen: A user attributes an underperforming page solely to backlinks
Explaining why a technically sound page may still not rank
doesNotApplyWhen: Claiming links do not matter - Google calls PageRank one of its fundamental algorithms
items.recommendedAction: Acknowledge links as one signal among many, and direct the user to the concrete issues the crawl actually found.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on - PageRank
source.quote: While PageRank uses links and is one of the fundamental algorithms at Google, there's much more to Google Search than just links. We have many ranking signals, and PageRank is just one of those.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google confirms PageRank is real and fundamental; this item counters over-attribution, not the existence of link-based signals.

items.title: Content length alone does not matter for ranking
items.principle: Google states that the length of the content alone does not matter for ranking purposes, that there is no magical word count target, minimum or maximum, and adds only that you probably want to have at least one word.
items.explanation: Word count is usable as evidence that a page may be too thin to serve its purpose, but never as a target. SEO Maker's own thin-content threshold is a heuristic and must be described as one.
items.whyItMatters: SEO Maker's deterministic layer applies a word threshold. This item is what stops the AI layer presenting that internal threshold as a Google requirement.
appliesWhen: Reporting the result of a word-count check
A user asks how long their content should be
Deciding how to phrase a thin-content finding
doesNotApplyWhen: Pages that genuinely fail to answer the query, where thinness is a real problem regardless of count
items.recommendedAction: Phrase thin-content findings as "this page may not cover its topic fully" and name what is missing, rather than "this page is under N words". Never recommend padding to a number.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Things we believe you shouldn't focus on - Minimum or maximum content length
source.quote: The length of the content alone doesn't matter for ranking purposes (there's no magical word count target, minimum or maximum, though you probably want to have at least one word).
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Genuinely thin pages that fail to answer the query remain a real problem. Google also notes that varying wording naturally gives more chances to show up, which is about vocabulary, not length.

items.title: Valid structured data makes pages eligible for special search features
items.principle: Google states that valid structured data on a page makes the page eligible for many special features in Google Search results, including review stars and carousels, and points to a gallery of result types a page can be eligible for.
items.explanation: Eligibility is the correct word in every structured data recommendation. Adding markup does not produce a rich result; it makes one possible.
items.whyItMatters: Promising rich results after adding markup is one of the most common ways SEO tools mislead users, and the correction is a single word.
appliesWhen: A page has no structured data and could qualify for a supported feature
Explaining the benefit of adding or fixing markup
doesNotApplyWhen: Promising that a rich result will appear
Claiming structured data improves ranking
items.recommendedAction: Describe structured data as creating eligibility for named features, and say that display remains Google's decision and varies by query.

source.name: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
source.location: Section: Next steps - Enhance how your site looks in Google Search results
