source.quote: Valid structured data on your pages also makes your pages eligible for many special features in Google Search results, including review stars, carousels, and more.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/SEO Starter Guide - The Basics (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Feature availability changes over time and some feature types have been narrowed or retired. Google separately states structured data is not required for its generative AI features.

items.title: Google publishes explicit self-assessment questions for content and quality
items.principle: Google's helpful-content guidance lists content and quality questions creators should ask, including whether the content provides original information, reporting, research or analysis; whether it gives a substantial, complete or comprehensive description of the topic; whether it offers insightful analysis beyond the obvious; whether it adds substantial value rather than copying or rewriting other sources; whether the main heading or page title gives a descriptive, helpful summary without exaggerating; and whether it would be worth bookmarking, sharing or seeing referenced in a printed publication.
items.explanation: These are the concrete questions SEO Maker's AI layer should reason against when it has page content. They convert a vague thin-content flag into specific, answerable gaps.
items.whyItMatters: It is the most defensible grounding available for content recommendations, because the questions come from Google rather than practitioner inference.
appliesWhen: Page content is available and needs a quality judgement
Explaining why a page reads as low value despite passing technical checks
Generating specific content improvement suggestions
doesNotApplyWhen: Producing a numeric content score - Google publishes no scoring formula
Pages whose purpose is functional or transactional rather than informational
Claiming these questions map onto specific ranking systems
items.recommendedAction: Assess the page against the named questions and report the specific ones it fails, with what is missing rather than a generic quality verdict.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Self-assess your content - Content and quality questions
source.quote: If the content draws on other sources, does it avoid simply copying or rewriting those sources, and instead provide substantial additional value and originality?
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: A self-assessment framework, not a scoring formula. Google does not publish how these questions map to ranking systems, and answering them well guarantees nothing.

items.title: Google names observable expertise signals: sourcing, author background, and verifiable accuracy
items.principle: Google's expertise questions ask whether content presents information in a way that makes you want to trust it - such as clear sourcing, evidence of the expertise involved, and background about the author or publishing site through links to an author page or About page - whether the site would be seen as well-trusted or widely recognised as an authority on its topic, whether the content is written or reviewed by someone who demonstrably knows the topic, and whether it contains easily-verified factual errors.
items.explanation: Several of these are partially observable from a crawl: presence of bylines, author pages, an About page, and outbound citations. That makes them actionable rather than abstract.
items.whyItMatters: It turns credibility advice into checkable page and site features, which is exactly the kind of recommendation SEO Maker can make concretely.
appliesWhen: Content pages carry no byline or author information
The site has no About or contact page
Assessing credibility on a YMYL-adjacent topic
doesNotApplyWhen: Forum or social content where an alias is an acceptable identifier
Presenting these features as ranking factors rather than trust signals
items.recommendedAction: Recommend bylines that link to author background, a clear About page, and explicit sourcing for factual claims, scaled to how consequential the topic is.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Self-assess your content - Expertise questions
source.quote: Does the content present information in a way that makes you want to trust it, such as clear sourcing, evidence of the expertise involved, background about the author or the site that publishes it[?]
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: These are trust signals for readers and raters, not confirmed ranking inputs. Google states separately that E-E-A-T is not itself a ranking factor.

items.title: Google lists warning signs of search-engine-first content
items.principle: Google lists warning signs that content is made for search engines rather than people: content made primarily to attract search visits; producing lots of content across many topics hoping some performs; using extensive automation across many topics; mainly summarising others without adding value; writing about trending things you would not otherwise cover; leaving readers needing to search again; writing to a word count; entering a niche without real expertise for traffic reasons; promising answers to questions that have no answer; changing page dates to seem fresh without substantial change; and adding or removing content mainly to seem fresh.
items.explanation: Several of these are detectable at site level: large volumes of thin pages across unrelated topics, templated content, and date changes without content changes between crawls.
items.whyItMatters: It gives SEO Maker an official basis for site-level pattern findings that no single page check would surface, and names practices the tool must never recommend.
appliesWhen: A site shows a large volume of shallow pages across unrelated topics
Page dates change between crawls without corresponding content changes
A user asks about publishing volume or content refresh strategies
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuine content updates, which Google encourages
Large sites with real topical depth and a coherent purpose
items.recommendedAction: Where these patterns appear, name the specific one observed and recommend consolidation or genuine improvement. Never recommend date-stamp refreshes or volume publishing.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Avoid creating search engine-first content
source.quote: Are you producing lots of content on many different topics in hopes that some of it might perform well in search results?
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: These are self-assessment warning signs, not a classifier. A site can exhibit one without being search-engine-first, and Google publishes no threshold.

items.title: Google states directly that it has no preferred word count
items.principle: Among its search-engine-first warning signs, Google asks whether you are writing to a particular word count because you have heard or read that Google has a preferred word count, and answers parenthetically: "No, we don't."
items.explanation: This is a direct first-party denial, stronger than an absence of guidance. Any word-count target in a recommendation contradicts it.
items.whyItMatters: SEO Maker applies an internal thin-content word threshold. This item is the guardrail that keeps that threshold described as an internal heuristic rather than a Google expectation.
appliesWhen: A user asks how many words a page needs
Phrasing a thin-content finding
A competing tool has recommended a word-count target
doesNotApplyWhen: Pages that genuinely fail to cover their topic, where the problem is coverage rather than count
items.recommendedAction: State that Google has no preferred word count, then describe what the page is actually missing in substance.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Avoid creating search engine-first content
source.quote: Are you writing to a particular word count because you've heard or read that Google has a preferred word count? (No, we don't.)
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: The denial concerns a preferred count. It does not mean length is never a symptom of a page that fails to answer its query.

items.title: Myth: changing dates or churning content makes a site look fresh to Google
items.principle: Claim: updating page dates, or adding and removing content in volume, signals freshness and helps rankings. Reality: Google lists changing the date of pages to make them seem fresh when the content has not substantially changed as a search-engine-first warning sign, and answers the question about adding or removing content to seem fresh with "No, it won't."
items.explanation: Freshness recommendations must be tied to genuine content change. A date-only update is explicitly named as a warning sign.
items.whyItMatters: Automated date-bumping is a widespread tactic and is easy for SEO Maker to detect across two crawls, making this both a myth guard and a real finding.
appliesWhen: Published or modified dates change between crawls with no substantive content change
A user asks whether to re-date old posts
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuine updates, where showing an accurate updated date is correct and useful
Query types that genuinely demand current information, where real freshness matters
items.recommendedAction: Recommend updating content substantively and reflecting that honestly in the date. Explicitly advise against date-only changes.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Avoid creating search engine-first content
source.quote: Are you adding a lot of new content or removing a lot of older content primarily because you believe it will help your search rankings overall by somehow making your site seem "fresh?" (No, it won't)
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Freshness genuinely matters for some query types, and accurate update dates are useful to readers. The myth is that the date itself is the lever.

items.title: Trust is the most important part of E-E-A-T, and not all four are needed
items.principle: Google states that of the E-E-A-T aspects, trust is most important; the others contribute to trust, and content does not necessarily have to demonstrate all of them - some content may be helpful because of the experience it demonstrates, other content because of the expertise it shares.
items.explanation: This prevents a checklist reading of E-E-A-T. A first-hand experience page does not need formal credentials to be strong, and a credentialed page that is untrustworthy is not saved by its expertise.
items.whyItMatters: It stops SEO Maker recommending credentials for content whose value is experiential, which is a common and unhelpful piece of automated advice.
appliesWhen: Explaining content credibility for a page
Deciding whether to recommend expert authorship or first-hand detail
doesNotApplyWhen: Treating E-E-A-T as a score or ranking factor
Clear YMYL topics where Google indicates some information genuinely requires expertise
items.recommendedAction: Identify which of experience or expertise the page's purpose actually calls for, and recommend strengthening that one rather than all four.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Get to know E-E-A-T and the quality rater guidelines
source.quote: Of these aspects, trust is most important. The others contribute to trust, but content doesn't necessarily have to demonstrate all of them.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: E-E-A-T is a rater and self-assessment concept. Google states it is not itself a ranking factor and there is no E-E-A-T score in its systems.

items.title: Google gives more weight to strong E-E-A-T signals on YMYL topics
items.principle: Google states that its systems give even more weight to content that aligns with strong E-E-A-T for topics that could significantly impact the health, financial stability or safety of people, or the welfare or well-being of society - the topics it calls Your Money or Your Life.
items.explanation: Business and topic context changes severity. The same thin, unsourced page is a materially more serious finding on a medical, financial or safety site than on a hobby blog.
items.whyItMatters: It gives SEO Maker a source-backed basis for scaling issue severity by the site's subject matter rather than treating every site identically.
appliesWhen: The site or page covers health, finance, safety, or civic topics
Prioritising content-credibility findings across a site
doesNotApplyWhen: Clearly non-YMYL topics, where Google indicates high accuracy and trust are not required to prevent harm
Implying a YMYL classification produces a penalty - it raises the standard, not a sanction
relatedIssues: low credibility on a YMYL topic
items.recommendedAction: Raise the severity of credibility, sourcing and accuracy findings when the site's topic is YMYL, and say why the standard is higher.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Get to know E-E-A-T and the quality rater guidelines
source.quote: our systems give even more weight to content that aligns with strong E-E-A-T for topics that could significantly impact the health, financial stability, or safety of people, or the welfare or well-being of society.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: YMYL is a spectrum judged by potential harm, not a fixed list of industries, and Google does not publish how the extra weight is applied.

items.title: Rater data is not used directly in ranking algorithms
items.principle: Google states that search raters have no control over how pages rank and that rater data is not used directly in its ranking algorithms; the analogy given is a restaurant collecting feedback cards from diners, used to know whether the systems seem to be working.
items.explanation: The rater guidelines are a legitimate source of vocabulary and evaluation criteria, but nothing in them is a ranking factor. SEO Maker should cite them as a quality rubric, never as algorithm behaviour.
items.whyItMatters: Much SEO advice cites the rater guidelines as though they described the algorithm. This distinction is what keeps SEO Maker's use of them honest.
appliesWhen: Citing rater guidelines concepts such as Page Quality, Needs Met, or E-E-A-T
A user asks whether raters can affect their site
doesNotApplyWhen: Dismissing the guidelines - Google says reading them helps creators self-assess and align conceptually with the signals its systems use
items.recommendedAction: When using rater-guideline concepts, label them as evaluation criteria that describe quality conceptually, not as ranking mechanics.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Get to know E-E-A-T and the quality rater guidelines
source.quote: Search raters have no control over how pages rank. Rater data is not used directly in our ranking algorithms.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google does say the guidelines help align content conceptually with the signals its automated systems use, so they are not irrelevant to ranking - only not directly used.

items.title: Google's Who, How and Why framework, with Why the most important
items.principle: Google asks creators to evaluate content by Who created it, How it was created, and Why it was created. It strongly encourages accurate authorship information such as bylines where readers would expect them, suggests explaining production methods where relevant, and states that Why is perhaps the most important question: the reason should be to help people, not primarily to attract search visits.
items.explanation: Who is partly observable from a crawl through bylines and author pages. How and Why are judgements the AI layer can make from content. The framework gives a consistent structure for explaining content recommendations.
items.whyItMatters: It is a compact, official structure for organising content feedback, and it ties credibility recommendations to something more concrete than 'improve quality'.
appliesWhen: Structuring content feedback for a page or site
Content lacks author attribution where readers would expect it
Assessing whether content exists for readers or for search
doesNotApplyWhen: Pages where a byline would not be expected, such as product or category pages
Forum or social content where an alias suffices
items.recommendedAction: Where bylines would be expected, recommend adding them with links to author background. Frame content recommendations around who made it, how, and why.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Ask "Who, How, and Why" about your content
source.quote: We strongly encourage adding accurate authorship information, such as bylines to content where readers might expect it.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: A self-assessment structure, not a ranking mechanism. Google gives no rule for when a byline is expected beyond reader expectation.

items.title: Disclose AI or automation where a reader would reasonably wonder how content was made
items.principle: Google states that a How component may include automated, AI-generated and AI-assisted content, asks whether the use of automation is self-evident to visitors through disclosures, and says AI or automation disclosures are useful for content where someone might think "How was this created?", to be added when it would be reasonably expected.
items.explanation: This is a conditional recommendation, not a blanket disclosure requirement. The trigger is reader expectation, which depends on the content type.
items.whyItMatters: SEO Maker generates content suggestions itself, so it needs an accurate position on AI disclosure - neither alarmist nor silent.
appliesWhen: Content was substantially generated or assisted by automation
A user asks whether they must disclose AI use
doesNotApplyWhen: Ordinary tool-assisted writing where readers would not wonder about production method
Claiming disclosure is required for indexing or ranking - Google frames it as useful, not mandatory
items.recommendedAction: Recommend disclosure where readers would reasonably ask how the content was made, and explain that it is a reader-trust measure rather than a ranking requirement.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: How (the content was created)
source.quote: Overall, AI or automation disclosures are useful for content where someone might think "How was this created?" Consider adding these when it would be reasonably expected.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google says to consider adding disclosures when reasonably expected; it does not define when that is, or state any search consequence for omitting them.

items.title: The spam line is purpose, not production method
items.principle: Google states that if you use automation, including AI generation, to produce content for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings, that is a violation of its spam policies on scaled content abuse.
items.explanation: The trigger is the primary purpose of the content, not the tooling. This is the precise boundary SEO Maker should use whenever AI-assisted content comes up.
items.whyItMatters: SEO Maker produces content recommendations with AI. Stating the boundary accurately protects users from both over-caution and genuine spam risk.
appliesWhen: A user asks about publishing AI-assisted content
A site shows large volumes of automated content across many topics
doesNotApplyWhen: AI-assisted content produced to genuinely help an audience, which Google does not treat as a violation
items.recommendedAction: Frame the question as purpose and added value. Recommend human review and genuine original contribution rather than avoiding automation.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Why (was the content created)
source.quote: If you use automation, including AI-generation, to produce content for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings, that's a violation of our spam policies.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google does not publish a volume threshold or a way to determine primary purpose from the outside, so this supports reasoning rather than classification.

items.title: Page experience is assessed across many aspects, not one or two metrics
items.principle: Google states that its core ranking systems look to reward content that provides a good page experience, and that site owners should not focus on only one or two aspects of page experience but check whether they provide an overall great page experience across many aspects.
items.explanation: This is the correct framing for performance findings. A Core Web Vitals number is one input to page experience, not the whole of it, and chasing a single metric is explicitly discouraged.
items.whyItMatters: It stops performance recommendations being presented as the dominant lever and keeps them proportionate to content and technical findings.
appliesWhen: Reporting performance or Core Web Vitals findings
A user asks whether improving one metric will improve rankings
doesNotApplyWhen: Diagnosing a specific metric regression, where narrow focus is appropriate for the diagnosis itself
items.recommendedAction: Present performance findings as one component of page experience, alongside mobile rendering, intrusive interstitials and main-content clarity.

source.name: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
source.location: Section: Provide a great page experience
source.quote: Site owners seeking to be successful with our systems should not focus on only one or two aspects of page experience. Instead, check if you're providing an overall great page experience across many aspects.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google does not enumerate every aspect of page experience or publish weights, so this guides framing rather than scoring.

items.title: Google's generative AI features run on its core Search ranking and quality systems
items.principle: Google states that SEO best practices continue to be relevant because its generative AI features on Google Search are rooted in its core Search ranking and quality systems, and that these features use AI techniques to highlight content from the Search index. It adds that from Google Search's perspective, optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience, and thus still SEO.
items.explanation: SEO Maker's GEO module should therefore build on the same deterministic checks as its SEO module, not a parallel ruleset. There is no separate technical discipline to sell.
items.whyItMatters: It is the anchor fact for the whole GEO area: it tells the AI layer to reuse existing evidence rather than invent AI-specific requirements.
appliesWhen: A user asks how to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode
Deciding whether a GEO finding needs its own check or reuses an SEO one
Evaluating third-party AEO or GEO advice
doesNotApplyWhen: AI assistants outside Google, which have not made equivalent statements
Claiming that ranking in classic results guarantees inclusion in an AI response
items.recommendedAction: Answer AI-visibility questions with the site's existing SEO evidence, and say explicitly that Google treats generative AI optimisation as SEO.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Is SEO still relevant for generative AI search?
source.quote: From Google Search's perspective, optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience, and thus still SEO.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: This describes Google's features only. Other AI assistants retrieve differently, and Google does not publish how sources are selected among eligible results.

items.title: Eligibility for Google's AI features needs indexing, snippet eligibility, and Search Console inclusion
items.principle: Google states that to be eligible to be shown in generative AI features on Google Search, a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet, fulfilling the Search technical requirements. It adds that in addition to those technical requirements, a site must be included in Search generative AI features in Search Console to be eligible for display.
items.explanation: There are three conditions, and the third is a Search Console setting rather than an on-site property. SEO Maker can verify the first two from a crawl but cannot observe the third, so it should name it as a manual check the user must perform.
items.whyItMatters: The Search Console condition is newer than most GEO advice in circulation. A site can be perfectly indexable and still be ineligible, and no crawl-based tool can detect that.
appliesWhen: A user asks why their content does not appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode
Producing a GEO readiness assessment
A page carries nosnippet or max-snippet directives
doesNotApplyWhen: Non-Google AI assistants
Treating eligibility as a guarantee of appearing - Google states indexing and serving are not guaranteed
items.recommendedAction: Verify indexability and snippet eligibility from the crawl, then tell the user to confirm the site's inclusion in Search generative AI features in Search Console, which the tool cannot check.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Build and maintain a clear technical structure - Meet the Search technical requirements
source.quote: In addition to the technical requirements for Search, a site must be included in Search generative AI features in Search Console to be eligible for display in generative AI features on Google Search.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Meeting all conditions does not guarantee appearance. Google states plainly that meeting requirements does not mean it will crawl, index or serve the content. This condition is specific to Google.

items.title: Meeting every requirement does not guarantee crawling, indexing or serving
items.principle: Google states that just because a page meets all requirements, best practices and policies does not mean Google will crawl, index or serve its content - indexing and serving are not guaranteed.
items.explanation: This is the caveat that belongs on any recommendation SEO Maker makes about visibility. The tool can remove obstacles; it cannot promise outcomes.
items.whyItMatters: It is the single clearest first-party statement against outcome promises, and it applies to SEO and GEO recommendations alike.
appliesWhen: Phrasing the expected result of any indexing or visibility recommendation
A user asks whether a fix will get them indexed or cited
doesNotApplyWhen: Reporting a verifiable current state, such as the page's status code or robots directives
items.recommendedAction: Phrase recommendations as removing obstacles and improving the chance of inclusion, never as guaranteeing indexing, ranking or citation.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Build and maintain a clear technical structure
source.quote: Just because a page meets all requirements, best practices, and complies with the policies, doesn't mean that Google will crawl, index, or serve its content. Indexing and serving aren't guaranteed.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: A statement about guarantees, not about likelihood. Following the requirements does still make inclusion more likely.

items.title: Non-commodity content with a unique point of view is Google's top generative-AI recommendation
items.principle: Google states that creating content people find unique, compelling and useful will likely influence a site's presence in generative AI search more than any other suggestion in its guide. It contrasts commodity content based on common knowledge - its example is "7 Tips for First-Time Homebuyers" - with non-commodity content offering unique expert or experienced takes, exemplified by "Why We Waived the Inspection & Saved Money: A Look Inside the Sewer Line". It adds that a first-hand review provides a unique perspective, whereas a summary of existing content simply restates what is already available, and advises not recycling what others have said or what a generative AI model could easily produce.
items.explanation: This is the most specific first-party content guidance available for AI visibility, and it is assessable from page content: does this page contain something only this author could have written?
items.whyItMatters: It replaces vague GEO structural advice with a concrete, quotable content test, ranked by Google above every technical suggestion in the same guide.
appliesWhen: A page restates widely available information without first-hand input
A user asks how to improve their chances of appearing in AI answers
Generating content recommendations for a competitive informational topic
doesNotApplyWhen: Pages whose purpose is functional, transactional or navigational rather than informational
Reference pages where restating established facts accurately is the point
items.recommendedAction: Identify what first-hand experience, data or perspective the author has that the page does not yet show, and recommend adding that rather than restructuring or lengthening the page.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Create valuable, non-commodity content for your audience
source.quote: Don't just recycle what others on the internet have already said, or could easily be produced by a generative AI model.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google describes influence in the long run and gives no measurement. Judging commodity versus non-commodity requires reading the content and knowing the topic.

items.title: Organise content with paragraphs, sections and headings for readers, not for machines
items.principle: Google advises writing content for a human audience, making sure it is well written and easy to follow, and notes that people generally appreciate web pages organised by paragraphs and sections with headings that provide a clear structure to navigate content.
items.explanation: Structural advice is justified by reader benefit. This is the legitimate version of the popular claim that content should be restructured for AI extraction - Google endorses the structure, but for people.
items.whyItMatters: It lets SEO Maker recommend headings and sectioning honestly while refusing the adjacent myth that content must be chunked for machines.
appliesWhen: A page presents long unbroken content with no sectioning
Recommending heading structure improvements
doesNotApplyWhen: Recommending structure specifically so AI systems can parse the page, which Google says is unnecessary
Short pages where sectioning would add nothing
items.recommendedAction: Recommend paragraphs, sections and headings on the grounds of reader navigation, and say explicitly that machine-oriented chunking is not needed.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Create valuable, non-commodity content for your audience
source.quote: People generally appreciate it when web pages are organized by paragraphs and sections, along with headings that provide a clear structure to navigate content.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google states separately that heading order and count do not matter from a Search perspective, so this supports having structure, not a particular hierarchy.

items.title: Creating pages for fan-out query variations is scaled content abuse
items.principle: Google states that creating separate content for every possible variation of how people might search - including targeting fan-out queries - primarily to manipulate rankings or generative AI responses violates its scaled content abuse spam policy, and adds that it is an ineffective long-term strategy because a high quantity of pages does not make a site higher quality or more relevant.
items.explanation: Fan-out is a retrieval mechanism, not a content plan. This closes off the most common tactical over-reaction to the query fan-out concept.
items.whyItMatters: Query fan-out is widely discussed and the obvious wrong inference - build a page per sub-query - is named by Google as a spam policy violation. SEO Maker must never suggest it.
appliesWhen: A user proposes creating pages per query variation or sub-question
A site shows many near-duplicate pages differing only by keyword variant
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuinely distinct pages that serve materially different user needs
items.recommendedAction: Advise covering a topic properly on one page rather than splitting it across query-variant pages, and name the spam policy risk explicitly.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Create valuable, non-commodity content for your audience
source.quote: While it might be tempting to create separate content for every possible variation of how people might search [...] doing so primarily to manipulate rankings or generative AI responses in Google Search violates Google's scaled content abuse spam policy.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: The violation turns on primary purpose being manipulation. Google publishes no page-count threshold, so this supports reasoning rather than automated classification.

items.title: Google's generative AI models ground responses on publicly accessible, crawlable content
items.principle: Google states that to maximise visibility in generative AI search features, site owners should ensure their content is crawlable, because Google Search generative AI models use publicly accessible, crawlable content to learn patterns and provide relevant, grounded responses.
items.explanation: Crawlability is the prerequisite for AI visibility, which means robots.txt and rendering findings are GEO findings too. The same evidence serves both analyses.
items.whyItMatters: It lets SEO Maker answer AI-visibility questions with technical evidence it already collects, rather than speculating about AI-specific factors.
appliesWhen: Content is blocked by robots.txt or requires authentication
A user asks why their content is not being used in AI answers
Auditing a large or frequently updated site for crawl efficiency
doesNotApplyWhen: Content deliberately kept private, where exclusion is the intended outcome
items.recommendedAction: Report robots.txt blocks and rendering obstacles as AI-visibility findings as well as SEO findings, and point large or frequently updated sites at crawl budget guidance.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Build and maintain a clear technical structure
source.quote: ensure your content is crawlable, as Google Search generative AI models use publicly accessible, crawlable content to learn patterns and provide relevant, grounded responses.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Crawlability is necessary, not sufficient. Google does not publish how it selects among crawlable sources when generating a response.

items.title: Perfect semantic HTML is not required; Google can understand imperfect markup
items.principle: Google states that it is not required to have perfectly semantic HTML - noting the web in general is not valid HTML and Google can understand it - while adding that it is generally a good idea to use semantic HTML where possible because it helps other users such as screen readers parse and navigate the page.
items.explanation: Markup validity findings should be reported as accessibility and maintainability improvements, not as search or AI requirements.
items.whyItMatters: HTML validation findings are easy to generate in volume and easy to overstate. Google's own position keeps their severity honest.
appliesWhen: A page uses non-semantic markup such as div-based structure
A user asks whether HTML validity affects search or AI visibility
doesNotApplyWhen: Markup problems that actually prevent content from rendering or being parsed
Accessibility audits, where semantic markup genuinely matters
items.recommendedAction: Report semantic HTML as an accessibility and agent-readiness improvement with low search severity, not as a requirement.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Build and maintain a clear technical structure
source.quote: While it's not required to have perfectly semantic HTML (the web in general is not valid HTML, and Google can understand it), it's generally a good idea to try to use semantic HTML when possible.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: This concerns validity and semantics. Content that genuinely fails to render, or is hidden behind blocked resources, remains a real problem.

items.title: Google can process JavaScript content as long as it is not blocked
items.principle: Google states that it is able to process content within JavaScript as long as it is not blocked, while noting that SEO on a site using JavaScript frameworks is generally more complex than on other kinds of sites, and pointing to its JavaScript SEO best practices.
items.explanation: JavaScript is not inherently a barrier. The two things that matter are whether the scripts are reachable and whether the rendered result contains the content.
items.whyItMatters: It prevents blanket warnings against JavaScript frameworks while preserving the real finding - blocked scripts - which SEO Maker can actually detect.
appliesWhen: A site renders main content with JavaScript
A user asks whether their framework hurts SEO or AI visibility
doesNotApplyWhen: Cases where scripts are blocked by robots.txt, which is a genuine defect
Content that never appears in the rendered DOM
items.recommendedAction: Check that scripts are not disallowed and that rendered output contains the main content, rather than advising against JavaScript.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Build and maintain a clear technical structure
source.quote: Google is able to process content within JavaScript as long as it isn't blocked.

items.limitations: Google acknowledges JavaScript SEO is more complex and has its own guidance; processable does not mean problem-free or equally fast.

items.title: Page experience matters for people arriving from AI features
items.principle: Google advises providing a good page experience for those who arrive at the site, including ensuring the site displays well across all devices, reducing latency, and making it easy for people to distinguish main content from other elements on the page.
items.explanation: Three named components: cross-device display, latency, and main-content clarity. The third connects directly to the rater-guideline concern about filler and distracting ads.
items.whyItMatters: It carries performance and layout findings into the GEO analysis with first-party justification, rather than leaving GEO as a content-only discussion.
appliesWhen: Reporting performance or mobile rendering findings in a GEO context
Main content is hard to distinguish from ads, navigation or promotional blocks
doesNotApplyWhen: Treating any single metric as the determinant of AI visibility
items.recommendedAction: Assess cross-device display, latency and main-content prominence together, and report them as page experience rather than as isolated metrics.

source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google gives no thresholds here and does not state how page experience affects generative AI feature inclusion specifically.

items.title: Merchant Center feeds and Business Profiles support product and local visibility in AI responses
items.principle: Google states that generative AI responses can include product listings, product information and information about local businesses where appropriate, and that using Merchant Center - including Merchant Center feeds - and Google Business Profiles can help products and services be visible in both AI responses and other Google Search results.
items.explanation: For commercial and local sites, some AI visibility depends on data supplied outside the website. SEO Maker cannot verify these from a crawl and should surface them as named off-site actions.
items.whyItMatters: It is the only concrete, first-party local and ecommerce GEO guidance in the source set, and it points at work the crawl-based analysis would otherwise miss entirely.
appliesWhen: The site sells products or serves a physical location
Producing GEO recommendations for a local business or ecommerce site
doesNotApplyWhen: Purely informational or non-commercial sites
Claiming a feed or profile guarantees inclusion in AI responses
items.recommendedAction: For commercial or local sites, recommend maintaining Merchant Center feeds and a Google Business Profile, and state clearly that these are off-site actions the audit cannot verify.

items.limitations: Google says these can help; it does not describe how the data is selected or weighted, and inclusion in AI responses is never guaranteed.

items.title: Google Search does not use llms.txt or any special AI markup file
items.principle: Google states that you do not need to create new machine readable files, AI text files, markup or Markdown to appear in Google Search including its generative AI capabilities, because Google Search itself does not use them. It adds that creating and maintaining LLMS.txt files for other services is fine and will neither harm nor help visibility or rankings in Google Search, as Google Search ignores them.
items.explanation: This is stronger than the seed item recorded: it covers any special machine-readable file or markup, not only llms.txt, and it explicitly states the neutral effect of publishing one anyway.
items.whyItMatters: llms.txt is among the most heavily marketed GEO tactics. A direct first-party denial lets SEO Maker decline to recommend it while answering the question accurately.
appliesWhen: A user asks about llms.txt or similar AI-oriented files
A third-party GEO audit has recommended adding one
The site already publishes an llms.txt
doesNotApplyWhen: Other AI providers, which have not made equivalent statements either way
Advising removal of an existing file, since Google says it neither harms nor helps
items.recommendedAction: State that Google Search ignores these files. Do not list llms.txt as a fix or attach any expected benefit to it, and do not recommend removing one that already exists.

items.limitations: The statement covers Google Search only, and the proposal is actively discussed, so the position should be re-verified periodically.

items.title: Content does not need chunking for AI, and there is no ideal page length
items.principle: Google states there is no requirement to break content into tiny pieces for AI to better understand it, that its systems can understand the nuance of multiple topics on a page and show the relevant piece to users, that sometimes shorter or longer pages work well depending on audience and subject, and that there is no ideal page length - pages should be made for the audience, not just for generative AI search.
items.explanation: This rules out two popular tactics at once: chunking for machine consumption, and targeting a page length. Structure remains worth recommending, but for readers.
items.whyItMatters: Chunking advice is a staple of GEO content marketing and would push users to restructure working pages for no stated benefit.
appliesWhen: A user asks whether to split content into smaller chunks for AI
A third-party GEO recommendation proposes restructuring for machine parsing
Discussing page length
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuinely unreadable pages, where sectioning helps human readers
Non-Google AI systems with different documented retrieval behaviour
items.recommendedAction: Decline to recommend machine-oriented chunking. Recommend structure only where it helps readers, and restate that there is no ideal page length.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Applies to Google's systems. Other retrieval systems may behave differently, and readability-driven structure is still endorsed.

items.title: Content does not need rewriting in a special style for AI systems
items.principle: Google states that you do not need to write in a specific way just for generative AI search, because AI systems can understand synonyms and general meanings of what someone is seeking in order to connect them with content that might not use the same precise words - so you do not have to worry about long-tail keywords or capturing every variation of how someone might seek your content.
items.explanation: This removes the basis for AI-specific rewriting services and for long-tail keyword coverage as a GEO tactic.
items.whyItMatters: Rewriting for AI is a commonly sold service. A direct denial lets SEO Maker steer users toward content substance instead.
appliesWhen: A user asks whether to rewrite content in an AI-friendly style
A recommendation proposes covering every query phrasing
doesNotApplyWhen: Rewriting for genuine clarity or reader benefit, which remains worthwhile
Non-Google systems
items.recommendedAction: Decline AI-specific rewriting recommendations. Redirect the user to substance, first-hand input and clarity for readers.

items.limitations: Applies to Google's systems. Writing clearly still matters, and the GEO research literature reports measurable effects from fluency changes on other engines.

items.title: Seeking inauthentic mentions across the web is not as helpful as it seems
items.principle: Google states that while its generative AI features can show what is being said about products and services across the web - including blogs, videos and forum discussions - seeking inauthentic mentions is not as helpful as it might seem, because its core ranking systems focus on high-quality content while other systems block spam, and its generative AI features depend on both.
items.explanation: Brand mention seeding is a widely marketed GEO tactic. Google acknowledges that mentions are visible to its AI features while explicitly discouraging manufactured ones.
items.whyItMatters: It lets SEO Maker respond accurately to mention-based GEO advice: the mechanism is real, the manipulation is not recommended.
appliesWhen: A user asks about seeding brand mentions for AI visibility
Evaluating a third-party GEO proposal built on mention volume
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuine PR, community participation or earned coverage
items.recommendedAction: Acknowledge that authentic discussion across the web is visible to AI features, and advise against manufacturing mentions.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

source.quote: However, seeking inauthentic "mentions" across the web isn't as helpful as it might seem.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google does not define inauthentic or describe how mentions are weighted, so this cannot support any quantitative recommendation.

items.title: Structured data is not required for generative AI search, but stays worthwhile for rich results
items.principle: Google states that structured data is not required for generative AI search and that there is no special schema.org markup that needs to be added, while adding that it is a good idea to continue using it as part of an overall SEO strategy because it helps with rich result eligibility on Google Search.
items.explanation: Both halves must travel together. Structured data keeps its classic justification and loses the AI-visibility justification that vendors often attach to it.
items.whyItMatters: Selling schema as the route into AI answers is a common overclaim, and the correction here comes with a legitimate reason to keep recommending markup.
appliesWhen: A user asks whether schema is needed for AI Overviews or AI Mode
Justifying a structured data recommendation
doesNotApplyWhen: Rich result eligibility, where required properties genuinely matter
Non-Google AI systems
items.recommendedAction: Recommend structured data for rich result eligibility only, and state plainly that it is not required for Google's generative AI features.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
