items.limitations: Applies to Google's AI features. Other AI systems have not documented equivalent positions, and structured data remains required for specific rich result types.

items.title: Search Console has a Generative AI performance report, and no third-party tool sees Google's internals
items.principle: Google directs site owners to the Generative AI performance report in Search Console to measure how content performs in generative AI features on Google Search and Discover. It separately warns to be wary of third-party tools that promise ranking success or claim to use internal Google metrics, stating that no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems.
items.explanation: There is a first-party measurement surface, and SEO Maker should point to it rather than estimating AI visibility. The warning also applies to SEO Maker itself, which should not claim internal access.
items.whyItMatters: It gives users a real measurement route and constrains how SEO Maker may describe its own numbers - an honesty requirement the product has to meet.
appliesWhen: A user asks how to measure AI visibility
Describing the basis of SEO Maker's own scores or estimates
A third-party report claims to use Google's internal metrics
doesNotApplyWhen: Non-Google AI assistants, which have their own or no measurement surfaces
items.recommendedAction: Point users at the Search Console Generative AI performance report for measurement, and describe SEO Maker's own outputs as derived from its crawl, never from Google's internal systems.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Measure visibility in generative AI features with Search Console
source.quote: No third-party tool has access to our internal ranking or AI systems.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: The report covers Google's features only. Report availability and metric definitions may change, and citations that produce no click may not be fully represented.

items.title: Browser agents read pages through screenshots, the DOM and the accessibility tree
items.principle: Google describes AI agents as autonomous systems that perform tasks on behalf of people, notes that browser agents may access a website to gather data by analysing visual renderings such as screenshots, inspecting the DOM structure and interpreting the accessibility tree, and points to agent-friendly website guidance and emerging protocols such as the Universal Commerce Protocol.
items.explanation: Agent readability depends on rendering, DOM structure and accessibility semantics - which is the one concrete reason semantic markup and accessibility work carry forward-looking value.
items.whyItMatters: It connects accessibility findings to an emerging, first-party-described consumption channel, giving them a second justification beyond compliance.
appliesWhen: A user asks about preparing a site for AI agents
Justifying accessibility or semantic markup work in a forward-looking context
Auditing transactional flows on a commerce site
doesNotApplyWhen: Presenting agent readiness as affecting current Google Search or AI Overview visibility
Sites with no transactional or data-gathering surface an agent would use
items.recommendedAction: Where relevant, note that accessibility and DOM clarity also serve browser agents, and label this as emerging rather than an established ranking or visibility factor.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Explore agentic experiences
source.quote: browser agents may access your website to gather the data they need to complete these tasks, such as analyzing visual renderings (like screenshots), inspecting the DOM structure, and interpreting the accessibility tree.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: Google frames this as something to explore if relevant and if you have extra time. There is no stated search or AI-feature benefit, and the protocols named are emerging.

items.title: Google says plenty of content succeeds with no overt SEO at all
items.principle: Google states that plenty of content thrives in Google Search, including generative AI experiences, without any overt SEO at all, and that site owners do not need to accomplish everything in its guide in order to succeed on Google Search.
items.explanation: A long audit findings list is not a list of obligations. This supports presenting recommendations as ranked opportunities rather than a compliance checklist.
items.whyItMatters: It counteracts the natural tendency of an automated audit to imply that every finding must be fixed, which erodes user trust and buries the findings that matter.
appliesWhen: Presenting a long list of audit findings
A user is overwhelmed by the volume of recommendations
Deciding how forcefully to phrase low-severity items
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuine blockers such as noindex on important pages or a 5xx robots.txt, which do need fixing
items.recommendedAction: Rank findings and make clear which few matter most, explicitly noting that the rest are optional improvements rather than requirements.

source.name: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
source.location: Section: Next steps: what to focus on
source.quote: plenty of content thrives in Google Search (including generative AI experiences) without any overt SEO at all, and you don't need to accomplish everything in this guide in order to succeed on Google Search.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/Optimizing for Generative AI Features on Google Search (Google Search Central).pdf

items.limitations: This is about proportion, not permission to ignore genuine defects. Google still documents the practices it recommends.

items.title: Page Quality is judged in three steps: purpose, harm, then how well it achieves that purpose
items.principle: Google's rater guidelines set out three steps: assess the true purpose of the page, and rate it Lowest if the purpose is harmful or designed to deceive people about its true purpose; assess the potential to cause harm, rating Lowest anything harmful, untrustworthy or spammy; otherwise rate based on how well the page achieves its purpose. Google describes steps 1 and 2 as a screening process applied before other quality considerations.
items.explanation: Purpose comes first. SEO Maker cannot assess a page's content usefully without first establishing what the page is for, which its page-type classification already begins to do.
items.whyItMatters: It gives content analysis a defensible order of operations and prevents a product or login page being judged by article standards.
appliesWhen: Assessing whether a page's content is adequate
Comparing pages of different types within one site
doesNotApplyWhen: Treating this as a ranking algorithm - it is a human evaluation rubric
Purely technical findings, which do not depend on page purpose
relatedIssues: content judged against the wrong standard
items.recommendedAction: Establish the page's purpose before judging its content, and state that purpose in the finding so the user can see the standard being applied.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 3.0 Overall Page Quality Rating, page 22
source.quote: Steps 1 and 2 are a screening process to quickly detect harmful content before other PQ considerations are applied.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria, not ranking mechanics. Google states rater data is not used directly in ranking algorithms and no single rating affects how a page ranks.

items.title: Page type does not determine quality
items.principle: Google states that as long as a page is created to help people, no particular page purpose or type is considered higher quality than another - encyclopedia pages are not necessarily higher quality than humor pages - and that there are highest and lowest quality pages of every type, including shopping, news, forum, video, error, PDF, image, gossip, humor and home pages.
items.explanation: SEO Maker should not apply article-style content expectations to functional pages. A currency converter, a login page or a category page can be excellent while containing very little text.
items.whyItMatters: Word-count and content-depth checks misfire badly on functional pages. This is the principle that tells the AI layer to suppress or reframe those findings.
appliesWhen: A low-text page is functional rather than informational
Reporting thin-content findings on product, category, login or tool pages
doesNotApplyWhen: Informational pages, where content depth genuinely matters for the purpose
items.recommendedAction: Use the page-type classification to decide whether a content-depth finding applies at all, and suppress or reframe it for functional pages.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 2.2 Understanding the Purpose of a Webpage, page 10
source.quote: The type of page does not determine the PQ rating--you have to understand the purpose of the page to determine the rating.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. Determining the true purpose of a page still requires judgement that an automated classifier may get wrong.

items.title: Page content divides into Main Content, Supplementary Content and Ads
items.principle: Google's guidelines classify all content on a page as Main Content - any part that directly helps the page achieve its purpose - Supplementary Content, which contributes to a good experience without directly achieving the purpose, such as navigation links, or Advertisements and monetization. Google states that the quality of the MC plays a very large role in the Page Quality rating.
items.explanation: This gives SEO Maker a vocabulary for distinguishing the content that matters from boilerplate. Word counts and content judgements should target the main content, not the whole DOM.
items.whyItMatters: Template-heavy pages inflate text metrics with navigation and footers. Separating MC from SC is what makes a thin-content judgement meaningful.
appliesWhen: Measuring or judging the substantive content of a page
A page's text volume comes largely from navigation, footers or sidebars
doesNotApplyWhen: Technical checks that legitimately consider the whole document
items.recommendedAction: Base content-quality judgements on the main content, and report navigation or footer text separately rather than counting it toward the page's substance.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 2.4 Understanding Webpage Content, pages 13-14
source.quote: Main Content is any part of the page that directly helps the page achieve its purpose. [...] The quality of the MC plays a very large role in the Page Quality rating of a webpage.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Google notes that user reviews and comments may be MC on some pages and SC on others, so the boundary requires judgement about the page's purpose.

items.title: The page title is part of the main content, and misleading titles are evidence of low quality
items.principle: Google's guidelines state that the title at the top of the page is part of the MC, that descriptive MC titles allow people to make informed decisions about what pages to visit and helpful titles summarise the MC. A page title that is slightly misleading, shocking or exaggerated is listed as justification for a Low quality rating, because of the poor experience when users see the actual content after arriving.
items.explanation: Title quality has a second, independent justification beyond the title link: mismatch between title and content is itself a quality defect. Google's examples include speculative sequel announcements and sensationalised headlines.
items.whyItMatters: It lets SEO Maker evaluate titles on accuracy against page content - a judgement the AI layer can make - rather than on length, which the deterministic layer cannot justify.
appliesWhen: A title overstates, sensationalises, or does not match the page's content
Generating or reviewing a title against the page body
A page uses clickbait phrasing
doesNotApplyWhen: Title length, which neither this nor Google's title-link documentation addresses
Legitimately dramatic subject matter accurately described
items.recommendedAction: Compare the title against the page's actual main content and flag exaggeration or mismatch as a quality problem, explaining the reader-experience reason.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 5.2 Low Quality Main Content, page 60; Section 3.1 PQ Rating Considerations, page 20
source.quote: Exaggerated or shocking titles are evidence of Low quality because of the poor user experience that results when users see the actual MC after reaching the page.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria rather than algorithmic behaviour. Judging exaggeration needs the page content and some topic understanding.

items.title: Main content quality is judged on effort, originality, talent or skill, and accuracy
items.principle: Google states that for most pages the quality of the MC can be determined by the amount of effort, originality, and talent or skill that went into creating it, and that for informational and YMYL pages accuracy and consistency with well-established expert consensus also matter. Effort includes building page functionality, and on forum or social pages the level of participation and depth of conversation counts as effort.
items.explanation: These four dimensions are a far more precise content rubric than a generic quality judgement, and they tell SEO Maker what to name when a page falls short.
items.whyItMatters: It converts 'this content is weak' into a specific diagnosis - no original input, no evident effort, inaccurate, or poorly executed - which produces a far more actionable recommendation.
appliesWhen: Judging whether page content is adequate for its purpose
Explaining why a page reads as low value despite adequate length
Generating specific content improvement recommendations
doesNotApplyWhen: Producing a score - these are qualitative dimensions with no published weighting
Applying a single standard across page types: Google says expected effort differs by purpose
items.recommendedAction: Diagnose weak content against effort, originality, skill and accuracy, and name the specific dimension that is lacking.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 3.2 Quality of the Main Content, page 21
source.quote: For most pages, the quality of the MC can be determined by the amount of effort, originality, and talent or skill that went into the creation of the content.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria with no published measurement. Google explicitly says expectations differ by page type, and that talent or skill should be judged leniently for ordinary people sharing content.

items.title: Typical and average pages on a topic are Medium quality, not High
items.principle: Google instructs raters to have high standards and to calibrate by finding other pages on the same topic, stating that typical and average pages on a topic generally have Medium, not High, quality main content. It also notes that Medium quality pages are commonly found online.
items.explanation: Competitive calibration is built into the rubric. A page that merely matches what everyone else publishes is average by definition, which is exactly the commodity-content problem Google's generative AI guidance describes.
items.whyItMatters: It gives SEO Maker a principled reason to recommend differentiation rather than parity, and sets a realistic bar so that most pages are not reported as failures.
appliesWhen: A page covers a topic adequately but adds nothing beyond competing pages
Setting expectations about what a content recommendation can achieve
doesNotApplyWhen: Implying Medium quality is a defect - Google describes it as common and acceptable
Pages whose purpose is served perfectly well by standard treatment
items.recommendedAction: Where a page matches rather than exceeds what competitors publish, recommend a specific differentiator, and be clear that adequate is not the same as a defect.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 7.1 High Quality Main Content, page 72; Section 3.0, page 22
source.quote: "typical" and "average" pages on a topic generally have Medium (not High) quality MC.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater calibration guidance, not a ranking threshold. Google states a page can still be High quality without reputation information, and that Medium is common.

items.title: The most helpful main content should be near the top; prominent filler is a quality defect
items.principle: Google states that site owners should place the most helpful and essential MC near the top of the page so visitors can immediately access it, and that a high quality page has the most helpful MC placed most prominently. Filler - low-effort content that adds little value and does not directly support the purpose - can artificially inflate content and creates a poor experience, especially when placed prominently ahead of helpful content. A Low rating applies where there is a large amount of unhelpful filler, or visually prominent filler that makes the helpful MC hard to find.
items.explanation: This is the guideline behind the familiar complaint about recipe pages: the recipe belongs near the top. Content placement, not just content presence, is assessed.
items.whyItMatters: It gives SEO Maker a source-backed way to address pages that pass a word-count check precisely because they are padded - the opposite failure from thin content.
appliesWhen: A page buries its main content beneath long preambles or background
A page has high word count but low substance
Recommending content structure for a page that already has enough text
doesNotApplyWhen: Supporting content placed appropriately lower on the page, which Google says can still be valuable
Content types where a build-up is genuinely part of the purpose, such as narrative writing
items.recommendedAction: Recommend moving the page's core answer or content to the top and demoting supporting material, rather than adding more content.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 5.2.2 Filler as a Poor User Experience, page 61
source.quote: Web site owners and content creators should place the most helpful and essential MC near the top of the page so that visitors can immediately access it.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. Google distinguishes valuable supporting content placed appropriately from filler, which requires judgement about the page's purpose.

items.title: Having ads is not a quality problem; ads that obstruct the main content are
items.principle: Google states that the presence or absence of Ads is not by itself a reason for a High or Low quality rating, because without advertising and monetization some webpages could not exist. However, pages with Ads, SC or other features that significantly distract from or make it difficult to access the MC should typically be given a Low rating even if some of the MC is helpful. Google names difficult-to-close ads that follow page scrolls and interstitials requiring an app download as genuinely distracting, while a single pop-over with a clear close button is not.
items.explanation: The distinction is obstruction, not monetization. SEO Maker should never report ad presence or density as a quality problem in itself.
items.whyItMatters: Ad-density findings are easy to generate and easy to get wrong, and getting this wrong tells publishers their business model is a defect.
appliesWhen: A page has intrusive interstitials or sticky ads over the main content
Reporting anything about a page's advertising
doesNotApplyWhen: Ads that are visible but do not obstruct the main content
Counting ads as a quality metric
items.recommendedAction: Report advertising only where it obstructs access to the main content, and describe the obstruction rather than the ad count.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 2.4.3, page 15; Section 5.3 Distracting Ads/SC, page 62
source.quote: The presence or absence of Ads is not by itself a reason for a High or Low quality rating.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. Obstruction is a rendered-layout judgement that a crawl may not capture, and Google also holds sites responsible for the overall quality of the ads they display.

items.title: It should be clear who runs the site and who created the page's content
items.principle: Google states that for every page it should be clear who is responsible for the website and who created the content, noting that on forums and social platforms an alias or username is an acceptable way to identify the creator. An unsatisfying amount of information about the website or content creator for the page's purpose is listed as justification for a Low rating, and inadequate information for the purpose can contribute to a Lowest rating.
items.explanation: Presence of About, contact and author information is partly observable from a crawl, and the standard scales with the page's purpose - a store handling payments is held to more than a hobby blog.
items.whyItMatters: It is one of the few content-credibility criteria SEO Maker can partly verify structurally, and it matters most on exactly the sites where the stakes are highest.
appliesWhen: A site has no About, contact or author information
An ecommerce site lacks customer service information
Assessing credibility on a YMYL-adjacent site
doesNotApplyWhen: Forum or social pages where an alias is sufficient
Applying a uniform standard regardless of the page's purpose
items.recommendedAction: Recommend clear ownership, contact and authorship information scaled to the site's purpose, and treat missing customer service information on transactional sites as higher severity.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 2.5.2, page 19; Section 5.5, page 63
source.quote: Every page belongs to a website, and it should be clear: Who [...] is responsible for the website. Who [...] created the content on the page you are evaluating.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. Google notes that different locales and platforms have their own conventions for what information should be available.

items.title: Where a site's self-description conflicts with independent sources, trust the independent sources
items.principle: Google instructs raters to look for reputation information from outside, independent sources, and states that when there is disagreement between what the website or content creators say about themselves and what reputable independent sources say, the independent sources should be trusted. Reputation research should be performed according to the topic of the page.
items.explanation: On-site claims of authority carry little weight on their own. This also means reputation is topic-specific: a site trusted for one subject is not automatically trusted for another.
items.whyItMatters: It stops SEO Maker treating on-page authority claims - awards, credentials, trust badges - as evidence, and frames reputation as something earned off-site.
appliesWhen: A page makes strong on-site claims about its own authority
Assessing whether a site is credible for its topic
A site has branched into a topic outside its established area
doesNotApplyWhen: Small sites with little reputation information, which Google says can still be High quality
Treating absence of reputation information as negative
items.recommendedAction: Describe reputation as earned externally and topic-specific, and avoid citing on-page self-description as evidence of credibility.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 2.5 Understanding the Website, page 18; Section 3.3, page 23
source.quote: When there is disagreement between what the website or content creators say about themselves and what reputable independent sources say, trust the independent sources.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria requiring off-site research that a crawl-based tool cannot perform. Google explicitly says a page can be High quality with no reputation information available.

items.title: A conflict of interest undermines trustworthiness, including in reviews
items.principle: Google states that a website or content creator may not be a trustworthy source where there is a clear conflict of interest: product reviews by people who own the product and share their experiences can be very valuable, but reviews by the product manufacturer, or by an influencer paid to promote the product, are not as trustworthy.
items.explanation: Self-reviews and undisclosed paid endorsements are a credibility problem with a named mechanism. This matters on ecommerce and affiliate sites where reviews are a core content type.
items.whyItMatters: Review content is central to many commercial sites, and this gives SEO Maker a precise reason to flag first-party or undisclosed sponsored reviews.
appliesWhen: A site reviews its own products or services
Review content carries no disclosure of a commercial relationship
Auditing affiliate or comparison content
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuine first-hand reviews by independent users, which Google describes as valuable
Clearly labelled product descriptions that do not present themselves as reviews
items.recommendedAction: Flag review content produced by the seller or by paid promoters, and recommend clear disclosure or independent sourcing.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 3.4 E-E-A-T, page 27
source.quote: "reviews" by the product manufacturer ("Our product is great!") or "reviews" from an influencer who is paid to promote the product are not as trustworthy due to the conflict of interest.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. Detecting undisclosed commercial relationships from a crawl is generally not possible, so this supports interpretation rather than detection.

items.title: Lacking E-E-A-T for the page's purpose cannot be offset by reputation or site type
items.principle: Google states that the Low rating should be used if a page lacks appropriate E-E-A-T for its purpose, and that no other considerations - such as positive reputation or the type of website - can overcome a lack of E-E-A-T for the topic or purpose of the page. Its examples include a restaurant review by someone who never ate there, skydiving instructions from a non-expert, tax forms on a cooking site, and a shopping page with minimal customer service information.
items.explanation: A trusted site publishing content outside its competence does not inherit credibility. This is the rater-side counterpart to the site reputation abuse policy.
items.whyItMatters: It gives SEO Maker a basis for flagging topic drift on otherwise strong sites, which is a common pattern when a brand expands into content marketing.
appliesWhen: A site publishes content well outside its established topic
Content requires expertise the creator does not evidently have
A transactional page lacks customer service information
doesNotApplyWhen: Content where first-hand experience rather than formal expertise is what the purpose calls for
items.recommendedAction: Flag content that falls outside the site's demonstrated competence and recommend either genuine expertise input or narrowing the topic scope.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 5.1 Lacking E-E-A-T, page 60
source.quote: The Low rating should be used if the page lacks appropriate E-E-A-T for its purpose. No other considerations such as positive reputation or the type of website can overcome a lack of E-E-A-T.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria, not an algorithmic rule. Judging required expertise depends on the topic and on the page's specific purpose.

items.title: YMYL divides into Health or Safety, Financial Security, Government Civics and Society, and Other
items.principle: Google's guidelines define four YMYL harm types: YMYL Health or Safety, covering mental, physical and emotional health and any form of safety; YMYL Financial Security, covering topics that could damage a person's ability to support themselves and their family; YMYL Government, Civics and Society, covering public interest, trust in public institutions, elections and voting; and YMYL Other. A topic is YMYL either because the topic itself is harmful or because harm could result if the content is inaccurate.
items.explanation: These four categories let SEO Maker classify a site's subject matter and scale content-credibility severity accordingly, rather than treating YMYL as a single yes-or-no flag.
items.whyItMatters: Business context is one of the inputs SEO Maker collects. This is the taxonomy that turns that context into differentiated severity.
appliesWhen: Classifying a site's topic area for severity weighting
Deciding how strict to be about sourcing and accuracy
doesNotApplyWhen: Treating YMYL as a fixed list of industries - Google describes it as a spectrum judged by potential harm
Implying a YMYL classification is itself a penalty
items.recommendedAction: Classify the site against the four YMYL harm types and raise credibility, sourcing and accuracy severity where it lands in a clear category.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 2.3 Your Money or Your Life (YMYL) Topics, page 11
source.quote: YMYL Health or Safety [...] YMYL Financial Security [...] YMYL Government, Civics & Society [...] YMYL Other
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Google stresses YMYL is a spectrum - clear YMYL, definitely not, or something in between - and says many or most topics are not YMYL.

items.title: Two questions decide whether a topic is YMYL
items.principle: Google offers two diagnostic questions: would a careful person seek out experts or highly trusted sources to prevent harm, and could even minor inaccuracies cause harm - if yes, the topic is likely YMYL; and is the specific topic one most people would be content casually consulting their friends about - if yes, it is likely not YMYL. Google also notes that many or most topics are not YMYL.
items.explanation: These questions are directly usable by the AI layer to classify a site's topic without needing an industry lookup table, and they produce a defensible explanation of the classification.
items.whyItMatters: Industry-based YMYL lists misclassify constantly. A harm-based test handles the ambiguous middle, which is where most real sites sit.
appliesWhen: A site's topic is not obviously YMYL or non-YMYL
Justifying why a severity level was raised for a given site
doesNotApplyWhen: Clear cases at either extreme, where the classification needs no reasoning
items.recommendedAction: Apply the two questions to classify the topic, and state the reasoning when raising severity so the user can see why the standard changed.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 2.3 Your Money or Your Life (YMYL) Topics, page 12
source.quote: Would a careful person seek out experts or highly trusted sources to prevent harm? Could even minor inaccuracies cause harm? If yes, then the topic is likely YMYL.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: A judgement aid for human raters. It gives no threshold and depends on understanding the specific topic, not just the industry.

items.title: On YMYL topics, lived experience and expert information serve different purposes
items.principle: Google states that pages sharing first-hand life experience on clear YMYL topics may be considered to have high E-E-A-T as long as the content is trustworthy, safe, and consistent with well-established expert consensus, while some types of YMYL information and advice must come from experts. Its examples contrast non-medical sleep tips from people who have been pregnant with which sleep medications are safe during pregnancy, and a forum discussion about coping with liver cancer treatment with treatment options and life expectancies.
items.explanation: A YMYL classification does not mean every page needs credentialed authorship. The distinction is whether the page gives information and advice or shares experience.
items.whyItMatters: Blanket 'add a medical reviewer' advice on every page of a health site is unhelpful and often wrong. This item lets SEO Maker target that recommendation where it belongs.
appliesWhen: A YMYL site contains both experiential and advisory content
Deciding whether to recommend expert authorship or review for a page
doesNotApplyWhen: Experiential content that contradicts well-established expert consensus, which Google does not excuse
Non-YMYL topics
items.recommendedAction: Distinguish experiential from advisory pages and recommend expert authorship or review only for the advisory ones, while requiring consistency with expert consensus throughout.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 3.4.1 YMYL Topics: Experience or Expertise?, page 28
source.quote: Pages that share first-hand life experience on clear YMYL topics may be considered to have high E-E-A-T as long as the content is trustworthy, safe, and consistent with well-established expert consensus.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. The boundary between sharing experience and giving advice requires judgement, and safety and consensus consistency apply to both.

items.title: Scaled content abuse is about value and purpose, not about how content was produced
items.principle: Google defines scaled content abuse as generating many pages primarily to benefit the website owner rather than help users, typically creating large amounts of unoriginal content providing little to no value compared to other similar pages on the web, no matter how it is created. Named examples include using automated tools including generative AI as a low-effort way to produce many low-value pages; scraping feeds or search results, including through synonymizing or translation; stitching content from different pages without adding value; creating multiple sites to hide the scaled nature of the content; and creating many pages that make little sense to a reader but contain search keywords.
items.explanation: The repeated phrase is no matter how it is created. Volume plus low value plus owner-benefit purpose is the pattern, and SEO Maker can observe the first two across a crawl.
items.whyItMatters: It is the precise definition behind Google's scaled content spam policy, and it lets SEO Maker discuss AI-assisted content risk accurately instead of vaguely.
appliesWhen: A site shows large volumes of templated or near-identical low-value pages
Content appears scraped, machine-translated or stitched from other sources
A user asks about publishing content at scale
doesNotApplyWhen: Large sites with genuinely distinct, valuable pages
Licensed or syndicated content, which Google says should not be considered copied
items.recommendedAction: Where volume and low value coincide, name the pattern and recommend consolidation or genuine added value. Never recommend scaled publishing.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 4.6.5 Scaled Content Abuse, page 41
source.quote: This practice is typically focused on creating large amounts of unoriginal content that provides little to no value for website visitors compared to other similar pages on the web, no matter how it's created.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater guidance on a spam policy, with no published page-count threshold. Google instructs raters to look at several pages of a site before concluding, and a crawl sample may not be representative.

items.title: Using generative AI tools alone does not determine content quality
items.principle: Google states that the use of generative AI tools alone does not determine the level of effort or the Page Quality rating: such tools may be used for high quality and low quality content creation. It gives creating high quality original artwork with generative AI as an example of high effort, while noting the same tools can produce Lowest quality content with little effort, originality or added value.
items.explanation: This is the strongest available statement that production method is not the criterion, and it comes from the same document that defines scaled content abuse - so both halves are authoritative.
items.whyItMatters: SEO Maker generates content suggestions with AI. It needs an accurate, quotable position that avoids both scaremongering and complacency.
appliesWhen: A user asks whether AI-assisted content will hurt their site
Recommending AI-assisted content production
Assessing content that appears machine-generated
doesNotApplyWhen: Unreviewed mass generation, which falls squarely under scaled content abuse
items.recommendedAction: State that the tool used is not the criterion, and direct the assessment to effort, originality and added value instead.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 4.6.6, page 42
source.quote: the use of Generative AI tools alone does not determine the level of effort or Page Quality rating. Generative AI tools may be used for high quality and low quality content creation.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Google states elsewhere that scaled low-value content remains a spam concern regardless of production method, so this does not license unreviewed generation.

items.title: Copying or paraphrasing is not automatically low quality; the test is effort, originality and added value
items.principle: Google states that copying, paraphrasing, embedding or reposting content does not automatically make a page Lowest quality, but that the Lowest rating is required when all or almost all of the MC is copied, paraphrased, embedded or reposted with little to no effort, originality and added value. Where there is low - rather than no - effort to add value by editing, curating, reformatting or injecting original content, the Low rating applies. Licensed or syndicated content, such as AP or Reuters news articles, should not be considered copied.
items.explanation: There is a graded scale here, plus an explicit syndication exemption. SEO Maker should not report content overlap as a defect without assessing what the page adds.
items.whyItMatters: Duplicate-detection findings are easy to produce and frequently wrong about syndicated or licensed content, which is entirely legitimate.
appliesWhen: Page content overlaps substantially with other pages on the web
A site republishes or aggregates third-party content
doesNotApplyWhen: Licensed or syndicated content, which Google explicitly exempts
A site's own duplicate URLs, which is a canonicalisation matter rather than an originality one
items.recommendedAction: Where content is reproduced, assess and report what the page adds. Treat syndication as legitimate and recommend added commentary, curation or original material where it is absent.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 4.6.6, page 42; Section 5.2.1, page 61
source.quote: Copying, paraphrasing, embedding or reposting content does not automatically make a page Lowest quality. [...] Licensed or syndicated content should not be considered as "copied".
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. Google acknowledges that identifying the original source is often difficult and that paraphrased content is much harder to recognise than copied content.

items.title: Expired domain abuse: repurposing a trusted domain for unrelated low-value content
items.principle: Google defines expired domain abuse as purchasing an expired domain and repurposing it primarily to benefit the new owner by hosting content of little to no value, often trading on the reputation of a former government, charity or school site. Its examples include affiliate content on a former government agency site, commercial medical products on a former medical charity site, and casino content on a former elementary school site. Google suggests checking the Internet Archive to confirm an obvious change of purpose.
items.explanation: The detectable signal is a mismatch between what the domain's URL structure and history imply and what the site now publishes. This is relevant when auditing an acquired domain.
items.whyItMatters: Domain acquisition is sometimes recommended as an SEO shortcut. This names it as a spam pattern and gives a concrete verification method.
appliesWhen: A site's current topic is inconsistent with its domain name or historical URL structure
A user asks about buying an expired domain for its existing authority
doesNotApplyWhen: Legitimate rebrands and business pivots that keep serving the audience
Domain purchases where the new site is genuinely valuable
items.recommendedAction: Where a domain's history and current content conflict, flag it and point to the Internet Archive as the verification route. Do not recommend acquiring domains for residual authority.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 4.6.3 Expired Domain Abuse, page 40
source.quote: Expired domain abuse is where an expired domain name is purchased and repurposed primarily to benefit the new website owner by hosting content that provides little to no value to users.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater guidance on a spam policy. A crawl alone cannot establish domain history, so this supports interpretation and a manual check rather than detection.

items.title: Site reputation abuse: third-party content hosted to borrow the host's ranking signals
items.principle: Google defines site reputation abuse as publishing third-party content on a host site mainly because of that host's already-established ranking signals, so the content ranks better than it could on its own. Third-party content alone is not abuse - it is abuse only when the reason for hosting it is the host's ranking signals. Named examples include payday-loan reviews on an educational site, casino pages on a medical site, and white-label coupons on a news site. Wire services, syndicated news, user-generated content sections, editorial columns and ordinary affiliate links are explicitly not site reputation abuse.
items.explanation: The detectable pattern is a section whose topic is unrelated to the rest of the site and which a reader would be surprised to find there. Google's own exclusion list prevents over-flagging.
items.whyItMatters: Hosted coupon, casino and comparison sections on established sites are a widespread pattern, and the exclusion list is what keeps SEO Maker from flagging legitimate syndication and UGC.
appliesWhen: A site hosts a content section clearly unrelated to its main topic
Sections appear to be operated by a third party or white-label provider
doesNotApplyWhen: Wire service or press release sites
Syndicated news, UGC sections, editorial columns, or advertorials shared directly with readers
Ordinary affiliate links or third-party ad units used throughout a page
items.recommendedAction: Flag topically unrelated hosted sections and check them against Google's exclusion list before reporting, naming which pattern applies.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 4.6.4 Site Reputation Abuse, pages 40-41
source.quote: Having third-party content alone isn't site reputation abuse; it's only site reputation abuse if the third-party content is published on a host site mainly because of that host site's already-established ranking signals.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: The violation turns on the reason for hosting, which is not observable from a crawl. Google's list of exclusions is broad and must be applied before flagging.

items.title: Hacked pages and heavily spammed comment sections are rated Lowest
items.principle: Google states that hacked, defaced or bot-spammed pages should be rated Lowest because they fail to achieve their original purpose, that responsible website owners should regularly check their sites for suspicious behaviour, and that if a specific page has many unrelated spammed comments - often posted by bots to advertise a product or create a link - the page should be rated Lowest.
items.explanation: Unmoderated comment sections are a real quality liability, not just an aesthetic one, and comment spam is partly observable from crawled page content and outbound link patterns.
items.whyItMatters: Abandoned comment sections accumulate spam silently on otherwise healthy sites, and this gives the finding a clear severity.
appliesWhen: Pages carry many unrelated comments with outbound commercial links
A site shows injected content inconsistent with its purpose
doesNotApplyWhen: Moderated comment sections with genuine discussion, which Google treats as contributing effort
items.recommendedAction: Flag pages with heavy comment spam and recommend moderation, closing old comment threads, and automatic link annotation for user-generated content.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 4.6.2 Hacked, Defaced, or Spammed Pages, page 39
source.quote: If a specific page on a website has many unrelated "spammed" comments, the page should be rated Lowest.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. Distinguishing spam comments from genuine discussion requires reading them, and a crawl may not capture comments loaded asynchronously.

items.title: Google's own intent taxonomy is Know, Know Simple, Do, Website and Visit-in-person
items.principle: Google's rater guidelines classify query intent as Know queries (finding information or exploring a topic), of which Know Simple queries seek a specific correct answer that fits in one or two sentences or a short list; Do queries, where the user wants to accomplish a goal or activity; Website queries, seeking a specific site or page; and Visit-in-person queries, seeking a business or a category of businesses. Google notes a query may have more than one of these intents and that the line between Do and Know is sometimes blurry.
items.explanation: This is Google's operational taxonomy and it differs from the classic three-class academic model. It adds a local intent class and separates simple-answer queries, both of which matter for page-type matching.
items.whyItMatters: Matching page type to intent is central to content recommendations, and using Google's own categories is more defensible than the industry's four-class variant.
appliesWhen: Assessing whether a page type matches the intent it targets
Classifying queries for content recommendations
A local business site is being audited
doesNotApplyWhen: Assuming intent can be read reliably from a query string alone
Treating the categories as mutually exclusive - Google says many queries do not fit neatly into one
relatedIssues: page type does not match intent
items.recommendedAction: Classify target intent with Google's categories and check the page type serves it, noting where a query carries more than one intent.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 12.7 Understanding User Intent, page 101
source.quote: Know query, some of which are Know Simple queries [...] Do query [...] Website query [...] Visit-in-person query
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria for human judgement. Google states the categories illustrate big-picture patterns and that many queries do not fit neatly into one.

items.title: Queries can carry several meanings, shift over time, and depend on user location
items.principle: Google states that many queries have more than one meaning - its example is mercury, which may mean the planet or the element - that user location informs intent, such as coffee shops meaning coffee shops in London for a London user, and that users are assumed to be looking for current information, so raters should think about a query's current meaning.
items.explanation: A single page cannot serve every interpretation of an ambiguous query, and the dominant interpretation can move. Recommendations built on one assumed meaning may be wrong.
items.whyItMatters: It sets a limit on how confidently SEO Maker should assert what a target query means, especially for short head terms and brand-adjacent words.
appliesWhen: A target query is short, ambiguous, or shares a name with something else
Content targets a term whose common meaning may have shifted
Local intent may be involved
doesNotApplyWhen: Unambiguous long-tail queries with a single clear reading
items.recommendedAction: State the assumed interpretation explicitly when making intent-based recommendations, and flag when a query plausibly carries other meanings.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 12.5-12.7, pages 98-101
source.quote: many queries also have more than one meaning. For example, if a user searches for "mercury," their intent may be to learn more about the planet mercury or the chemical element.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater guidance. Determining the dominant interpretation requires current search data that a crawl does not provide.

items.title: Four query types demand fresh content; for the rest, stale pages can still be high quality
items.principle: Google names four query types demanding current results: breaking news queries; recurring event queries such as elections, sports, TV shows and tax forms; current information queries such as populations, debt figures and airfares; and product queries, where users are assumed to want the most recent model or version. For these, pages about past events or outdated information are stale and should get low Needs Met ratings. Google adds that freshness is generally less of a concern for Page Quality: stale pages can have high Page Quality ratings, though unmaintained or inaccurate content is a reason for a low one.
items.explanation: Freshness is query-dependent, not a universal content property. This lets SEO Maker target refresh recommendations at the page types where recency actually matters.
items.whyItMatters: Blanket 'update your old content' advice wastes effort on evergreen pages. Naming the four query types makes the recommendation specific and defensible.
appliesWhen: A page targets news, recurring events, current figures, or products
Deciding which pages to recommend refreshing
Content references dated models, prices or years
doesNotApplyWhen: Evergreen or archival content, which Google says can be stale and still high quality
Recommending date changes without content changes
items.recommendedAction: Recommend refreshing only pages whose query type demands currency, and say why that page type needs it.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 18.0 Needs Met Rating and Freshness, page 158
source.quote: Freshness is generally less of a concern for Page Quality rating. "Stale" pages can have high Page Quality ratings.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria affecting Needs Met rather than Page Quality. Google also warns that the displayed date may not reflect when content was actually updated.

items.title: A landing page can be more or less specific than the query and still be helpful
items.principle: Google's guidelines discuss query specificity and state that the rating is based on how helpful the result is for the query, not on the specificity fit. A page more specific than a broad query can still be very helpful when it represents a popular or prominent option, while a page too specific for the query is a less helpful result. For broad category queries, popular and prominent examples may be considered very helpful.
items.explanation: There is no rule that a page must match a query's specificity level. Helpfulness is the criterion, which loosens the common advice to build a page per query granularity.
items.whyItMatters: It counters the reflex to recommend a new page whenever a query does not have an exact-match landing page, which feeds directly into content bloat.
appliesWhen: Deciding whether an existing page can serve a target query
A user proposes creating pages at every specificity level
doesNotApplyWhen: Pages so specific that they address an unlikely minor interpretation, which Google rates lower
items.recommendedAction: Judge whether an existing page can serve the query helpfully before recommending a new one, and explain the helpfulness reasoning.

source.name: General Guidelines (Search Quality Rater Guidelines)
source.location: Section 17.0 Specificity of Queries and Landing Pages, page 154
source.quote: As always, your rating is based on how helpful the result is for the query, not the specificity fit.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria. Google notes results for specific queries are easier to rate and that broad queries require web research to know what is popular and prominent.

items.title: No single rating or rater affects how a page ranks; ratings are used in aggregate
items.principle: Google's public overview states that no single rating and no single rater directly impacts how a page or site ranks, that using Search Quality Ratings for ranking purposes would not be feasible because humans could never rate every page on the open web, and that aggregated ratings are used to measure how well the systems are working and to give those systems positive and negative examples.
items.explanation: This is the scope boundary for everything drawn from the rater guidelines. SEO Maker may use them as a quality rubric and must not present them as ranking mechanics.
items.whyItMatters: A large share of the corpus comes from the rater guidelines. Carrying this boundary explicitly is what keeps that material honest in user-facing output.
appliesWhen: Citing any rater-guideline concept
A user asks whether a rater could have affected their site
doesNotApplyWhen: Dismissing the guidelines as irrelevant - Google says aggregated ratings shape system development
items.recommendedAction: Label rater-derived knowledge as evaluation criteria describing quality, never as ranking factors or algorithm behaviour.

source.location: Section 3: The Search Quality Rating Process, pages 16-17
source.quote: It is important to note that no single rating - or single rater - directly impacts how a given page or site ranks in Search.

items.limitations: The overview is dated November 2023 and is a summary document; the rater programme's scale figures may have changed since.

items.title: Needs Met measures usefulness for a query, with Fully Meets reserved for single-answer queries
items.principle: Google's Needs Met scale runs Fails to Meet, Slightly Meets, Moderately Meets, Highly Meets and Fully Meets. Fully Meets is described as a special category that applies only to queries with clear intent to find one specific result, and the corresponding specific result. Raters consider the extent to which a result fits the query, is up to date, is accurate and trustworthy for information-seeking queries, and satisfies the user.
items.explanation: Needs Met is result-and-query specific, while Page Quality is a property of the page. A high quality page can be a poor result for a given query, and this separation is exactly the distinction SEO Maker needs when a technically sound page underperforms.
items.whyItMatters: It gives the AI layer language for the most common real situation: the page is fine, but it is not the right answer to the query it targets.
appliesWhen: A technically sound, well-written page does not perform for its target query
Explaining the difference between page quality and query fit
doesNotApplyWhen: Treating the scale as a ranking output
Queries with no single intended result, where Fully Meets does not apply
items.recommendedAction: Separate page quality from query fit in findings, and where the page is sound, direct the recommendation at intent match rather than content quality.

source.location: Section 3: The Search Quality Rating Process, pages 28-30
source.quote: Fully Meets (FullyM): A special rating category, which only applies to queries with clear intent to find one specific result and the corresponding specific result the user is looking for.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/search quality rater guidelines an overview.pdf

items.limitations: Rater criteria from a November 2023 summary. The full guidelines carry the detailed definitions, and ratings do not directly affect rankings.

items.title: Broder measured roughly 20-25% navigational, 48% informational and 30% transactional queries
items.principle: Broder measured intent prevalence two ways on AltaVista. A user survey run between 26 June and 3 November 2001 with 3,190 valid returns found 24.5% navigational and 68.4% non-navigational, with transactional estimated at more than 22% and, from a 200-query sample with free-text explanations, around 36%. A separate log analysis of 1,000 randomly selected queries - reduced to the first 400 after removing non-English and sexually oriented queries - found 20% navigational, 48% informational and 30% transactional. The paper states that informational queries constitute less than 50% of web searches.
items.explanation: These are the origin figures for the intent distributions still quoted in SEO. They are useful as historical grounding and as an order-of-magnitude reminder that informational intent is a minority, but they describe one engine in 2001.
items.whyItMatters: SEO advice frequently cites intent percentages without provenance. Carrying the real numbers with their method lets SEO Maker cite them honestly or decline to.
appliesWhen: Discussing the historical basis of the intent taxonomy
A user cites intent distribution percentages and asks where they come from
doesNotApplyWhen: Estimating intent distribution for any current market, engine or vertical
Any site-specific or industry-specific intent modelling
items.recommendedAction: Cite these figures only with their date, engine and method attached, and do not use them to model a current site's query mix.

source.name: A taxonomy of web search
source.publisher: Andrei Broder, IBM Research - ACM SIGIR Forum 36(2)
source.location: Section 4 (Statistics), Figures 4 and 5
source.quote: Type of query | User Survey | Query Log Analysis. Navigational 24.5% | 20%. Informational ?? (estimated 39%) | 48%. Transactional > 22% (estimated 36%) | 30%.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/taxonomy of web search.pdf

items.limitations: AltaVista data from 2001, published 2002. The survey was self-selected with about a 10% response rate and Broder notes sexual-content queries were under 1% of survey responses against about 12% of the log, so the samples are not comparable. The two methods disagree, and the author describes log-derived intent inference as "very soft". Search behaviour, engines and the web have changed substantially.

items.title: Intent cannot be reliably inferred from the query text alone
items.principle: Broder states explicitly that there is no assumption that intent can be inferred with any certitude from the query, that the examples given might have alternative explanations, and describes inferring user intent from a query as at best an inexact science and usually a wild guess.
items.explanation: The author of the taxonomy everyone cites is explicit that the classification is not recoverable from the query string. Any intent label SEO Maker assigns is a hypothesis.
items.whyItMatters: Intent classification drives content recommendations. Treating a guessed label as fact produces confident but wrong advice about what a page should be.
appliesWhen: Assigning an intent label to a target query
Making a content recommendation that depends on assumed intent
doesNotApplyWhen: Queries where the intent is explicit, such as a brand name or an explicit transactional phrase
items.recommendedAction: Present intent classifications as inferences with stated reasoning, and note where an alternative reading is plausible.

source.name: A taxonomy of web search
source.publisher: Andrei Broder, IBM Research - ACM SIGIR Forum 36(2)
source.location: Section 3 (A taxonomy of web searches); Section 4 (Log analysis)
source.quote: Since inferring the user intent from the query is at best an inexact science, but usually a wild guess, the data obtained from log analysis is very "soft".
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/taxonomy of web search.pdf

items.limitations: A 2002 observation about query-log analysis. Modern engines use signals beyond the query string - location, history, context - that were not available to this analysis.

items.title: About 15% of searches sought a collection of links rather than a single best page
items.principle: Broder reports that in almost 15% of all searches the desired target is a good collection of links on the subject rather than a good document - a good hub rather than a good authority. The survey question found 14.83% wanting a site that is a collection of links on the topic against 76.62% wanting the best site on the topic.
items.explanation: A meaningful minority of searches want a curated resource list. This supports hub, directory and roundup page types as a legitimate response to some queries rather than as thin content.
items.whyItMatters: Link-collection and resource pages often trip thin-content checks despite serving a real and measured user need.
appliesWhen: A page is a curated resource list, directory, or hub
Deciding whether a link-heavy page is thin or purposeful
doesNotApplyWhen: Link pages with no curation or added value, which Google's guidelines treat as low quality
Estimating current demand for hub pages in any specific topic
items.recommendedAction: Judge curated hub pages by the quality of their curation rather than text volume, and note that a measurable share of searches seek exactly this page type.

source.name: A taxonomy of web search

items.limitations: AltaVista survey data from 2001 with self-selected respondents, in a pre-social, pre-app web. The figure should not be treated as a current proportion for any market.

items.title: Link analysis and anchor text were found especially effective for navigational queries
items.principle: Broder describes second-generation search engines as using off-page, web-specific data such as link analysis, anchor text and click-through data, and states that link analysis and anchor text seem crucial for navigational queries. He cites Craswell, Hawking and Robertson's SIGIR 2001 work showing anchor text provides very effective help for navigational queries.
items.explanation: Anchor text's measured value is strongest for finding a specific known destination. That is a narrower and better-supported claim than the general assertion that anchor text drives rankings.
items.whyItMatters: It gives internal anchor text recommendations a real evidence basis while keeping the claim within what the research supports.
appliesWhen: Explaining why descriptive internal anchor text matters
Auditing navigation and links to key destination pages
doesNotApplyWhen: Claiming anchor text drives rankings generally across query types
Recommending repetitive exact-match anchors
items.recommendedAction: Recommend descriptive anchors for important destination pages, framing the evidence as strongest for helping users and engines find a known destination.

source.name: A taxonomy of web search
source.publisher: Andrei Broder, IBM Research - ACM SIGIR Forum 36(2)

source.quote: Link analysis and anchortext seems crucial for navigational queries.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/seo/taxonomy of web search.pdf

items.limitations: A 2002 characterisation of second-generation engines, citing 2001 evaluations. Search engines have changed substantially and the paper offers no effect size for modern systems.

items.title: The GEO paper's headline results come from a simulated engine, not a production one
items.principle: The GEO paper's main experiments use a two-step setup the authors built: the top 5 sources are fetched from Google for each query, and gpt-3.5-turbo generates the response from those sources, sampled 5 times at temperature 0.7. Only a separate, smaller evaluation in Section 6 uses Perplexity.ai, a deployed generative engine. Visibility is measured with two metrics the authors define: Position-Adjusted Word Count, and Subjective Impression scored by GPT-3.5 using a G-Eval style template and then normalised to match the first metric's mean and variance.
items.explanation: This is the single most important scope fact about the paper. Its headline numbers describe a researcher-built pipeline and author-defined metrics, not measured behaviour of any commercial AI search product.
items.whyItMatters: Every GEO effect size in circulation traces back to this paper. Without the setup attached, those numbers read as measurements of AI Overviews or ChatGPT, which they are not.
appliesWhen: Citing any effect size from the GEO paper
A user cites GEO statistics from a vendor blog post
Assessing GEO advice that claims research backing
doesNotApplyWhen: The Perplexity evaluation in Section 6, which used a real deployed engine on a subset
items.recommendedAction: Whenever a GEO paper figure is cited, state the engine and metric it was measured on, and never present it as an expected uplift in a named commercial product.

source.name: GEO: Generative Engine Optimization
source.publisher: Aggarwal, Murahari, Rajpurohit, Kalyan, Narasimhan, Deshpande - KDD '24
source.location: Section 3.1 Evaluated Generative Engine; Section 2.2.1; Section 6
source.quote: The answer is then generated by the gpt3.5-turbo model [20] using the same prompt as prior work [14]. We sample 5 different responses at temperature=0.7, to reduce statistical deviations.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/GEO - Generative Engine Optimization (Aggarwal et al, KDD 2024).pdf

items.limitations: The metrics are proposed by the authors rather than validated externally, and Subjective Impression is scored by an LLM. The generator model, gpt-3.5-turbo, is several generations old.

items.title: GEO methods helped low-ranked sources most and reduced visibility for the top-ranked source
items.principle: The paper reports relative visibility change by the source's search ranking. For Cite Sources the change was -30.3% at rank 1 and +115.1% at rank 5; Quotation Addition was -22.9% at rank 1 and +99.7% at rank 5; Statistics Addition was -20.6% at rank 1 and +97.9% at rank 5. The authors conclude that GEO is especially helpful for lower ranked websites, and separately frame this as levelling the playing field for smaller sites.
items.explanation: The effect is not uniform and, for the already best-ranked source, it was negative in this setup. Advice derived from this paper should be conditioned on where the site already stands.
items.whyItMatters: It is the most consequential nuance in the paper and it is almost always dropped when the 40% headline is repeated. Applied to a market leader, the paper's own data suggests the tactics could cost visibility.
appliesWhen: Considering GEO content tactics for a site that already ranks well
A user cites GEO uplift figures without qualification
doesNotApplyWhen: Treating the rank-1 decline as an established effect in production engines - it is one measurement in one simulated setup
items.recommendedAction: When GEO tactics come up, note that the measured benefit was concentrated in lower-ranked sources and was negative for the top-ranked one in this experiment.

source.name: GEO: Generative Engine Optimization
source.publisher: Aggarwal, Murahari, Rajpurohit, Kalyan, Narasimhan, Deshpande - KDD '24
source.location: Section 5 (Analysis), Table 2
source.quote: Table 2: Visibility changes through GEO methods for sources with different Rankings in Search Engine. GEO is especially helpful for lower ranked websites.
source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/GEO - Generative Engine Optimization (Aggarwal et al, KDD 2024).pdf

items.limitations: Measured on the authors' simulated engine with their own visibility metric. The paper reports these as relative changes in a table without significance testing, and the mechanism is not explained.

items.title: Making content sound more authoritative produced no significant improvement
items.principle: The paper tested an Authoritative method that modifies text style to be more persuasive and authoritative. The authors report that although one would expect a more persuasive and authoritative tone to boost visibility, they find no significant improvement, demonstrating that generative engines are already somewhat robust to such changes, and conclude that owners should focus instead on improving content presentation and credibility.
items.explanation: This is a negative result against a widely marketed GEO tactic - writing with more authoritative phrasing. The measured lever was verifiable substance, not confident tone.
items.whyItMatters: Tone-rewriting is commonly sold as GEO work. A negative result from the field's founding paper is a useful counterweight.
appliesWhen: A user or vendor proposes rewriting content in a more authoritative voice for AI visibility
Evaluating GEO service offerings
doesNotApplyWhen: Genuine credibility improvements such as sourcing, data and author expertise, which the same paper found did help
items.recommendedAction: Decline to recommend authoritative-sounding rewrites. Redirect to verifiable substance: sources, quotations and data.

items.limitations: One method in one simulated setup, with no significance test reported. In the Perplexity evaluation the Authoritative method was not among those reported at all.

items.title: On Perplexity.ai the measured gains were smaller, and keyword stuffing performed worse than baseline
items.principle: Evaluated on Perplexity.ai, a deployed generative engine, Quotation Addition performed best on Position-Adjusted Word Count with a 22% improvement over baseline; Cite Sources and Statistics Addition showed improvements of up to 9% and 37% on the two metrics; and Keyword Stuffing performed 10% worse than the baseline on Position-Adjusted Word Count.
items.explanation: This is the only part of the paper measured against a real product, and the gains are roughly half the headline figure. It is the number to cite when a real engine is the subject.
items.whyItMatters: It is the closest thing in the corpus to evidence about a production AI search engine, and it moderates the headline claim considerably.
appliesWhen: Discussing what GEO research shows about a real deployed engine
A user asks whether GEO tactics work in practice
doesNotApplyWhen: Google's AI Overviews or AI Mode, which were not tested
Treating the Perplexity numbers as current - the evaluation predates June 2024
items.recommendedAction: When citing GEO evidence about deployed engines, use the Perplexity figures and name the engine and date, not the headline 40%.

source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/GEO - Generative Engine Optimization (Aggarwal et al, KDD 2024).pdf

items.limitations: A single engine at a single point in time before June 2024, on a test subset, using the authors' own metrics. Perplexity publishes no ranking or citation formula, and its systems have changed since. Notably, Keyword Stuffing scored above baseline on the Subjective Impression metric in the same table even while scoring 10% below on the primary metric.

items.title: Which GEO method worked best varied by subject domain
items.principle: The paper reports that the effectiveness of GEO methods varies across query domains and gives a per-method breakdown of top-performing categories: Authoritative performed best for Debate, History and Science; Fluency Optimization for Business, Science and Health; Cite Sources for Statement, Facts and Law & Government; Quotation Addition for People & Society, Explanation and History; and Statistics Addition for Law & Government, Debate and Opinion. The authors conclude that owners should make domain-specific targeted adjustments.
items.explanation: There is no single GEO tactic that works everywhere, even within the paper's own setup. Any blanket GEO checklist contradicts the source it usually cites.
items.whyItMatters: It undercuts one-size-fits-all GEO advice using the founding paper's own analysis, which is a strong position for SEO Maker to take.
appliesWhen: Evaluating a generic GEO checklist
A user asks which GEO tactic to apply to their topic
doesNotApplyWhen: Prescribing a specific method for a specific industry - the category labels are the paper's own and do not map cleanly onto real verticals
items.recommendedAction: Note that measured effectiveness varied by subject area, and decline to present a universal GEO tactic list.

source.localPath: knowledge/raw/geo/GEO - Generative Engine Optimization (Aggarwal et al, KDD 2024).pdf

items.limitations: Categories were assigned by GPT-4 with manual verification on the test split, and the authors acknowledge possible labelling discrepancies. Rankings of top categories are reported without effect sizes or significance tests.

items.title: GEO-bench is 10,000 queries, deliberately 80% informational
items.principle: GEO-bench comprises 10,000 queries split 8,000 train, 1,000 validation and 1,000 test, drawn from nine datasets including real anonymised user queries, AllSouls essay questions, Perplexity.ai Discover, ELI5, and GPT-4 generated queries. The authors state they preserve the real-world query distribution with 80% informational queries and 10% each transactional and navigational. Each query is augmented with cleaned text from the top 5 Google results, and queries span 25 domains.
items.explanation: The benchmark is heavily informational by design. Findings from it say little about transactional or navigational queries, which is where most commercial sites earn revenue.
items.whyItMatters: It bounds who the paper's conclusions apply to. An ecommerce site's key queries are barely represented in the dataset the GEO field is built on.
appliesWhen: Assessing whether GEO research applies to a particular site
A commercial or transactional site asks about GEO tactics
doesNotApplyWhen: Informational publisher content, which the benchmark does represent well
items.recommendedAction: Note the 80% informational composition when applying GEO findings to transactional or navigational content, and lower confidence accordingly.

items.limitations: A portion of the queries were generated by GPT-4 to supplement diversity. The claimed real-world distribution is asserted rather than independently validated, and the authors note query distributions change over time.

items.title: The GEO authors state they did not evaluate any effect on search rankings
items.principle: The paper's Limitations section states that owing to the black-box nature of search engine algorithms the authors did not evaluate how GEO methods affect search rankings, though they reason the changes are textual and do not affect metadata such as domain name or backlinks, so are less likely to affect rankings. They also note methods may need to adapt as generative engines evolve, query nature changes over time, larger context lengths may reduce the impact of search rankings, and query tagging may contain subjective or labelling errors.
items.explanation: The authors are explicit that the classic-search consequences of these content changes are unmeasured. Their expectation of neutrality is reasoning, not a finding.
items.whyItMatters: SEO Maker advises on both SEO and GEO. Recommending a GEO tactic without noting that its classic-search effect was never measured would misrepresent the evidence.
appliesWhen: Recommending any content change justified by GEO research
A user asks whether GEO tactics could hurt normal rankings
doesNotApplyWhen: Content changes justified by Google's own documentation rather than this paper
items.recommendedAction: State that the paper did not measure search-ranking effects, and prefer changes that are justified by official documentation as well as by the research.

items.limitations: This item records the authors' own stated limitations, which is a strength of the source rather than a weakness of the item. The neutrality expectation remains untested.

items.title: The best method combination was measured on only 200 examples
items.principle: The paper reports that combining GEO methods can enhance performance, with the best combination - Fluency Optimization plus Statistics Addition - outperforming any single GEO strategy by more than 5.5%. A footnote states that due to cost constraints this analysis was conducted on a subset of 200 examples from the test split, so the numbers differ from those in the paper's main results table.
items.explanation: The combination finding rests on a much smaller sample than the headline results and the authors flag it themselves. It should carry noticeably lower confidence.
items.whyItMatters: The combination figure circulates without its footnote. Carrying the sample size is what keeps the claim proportionate.
appliesWhen: A user cites the GEO method-combination finding
Assessing advice that stacks multiple GEO tactics
doesNotApplyWhen: The paper's main single-method results, which used the full test split
items.recommendedAction: Cite the combination result only with its 200-example sample size attached, and treat it as preliminary.
